The White Devil

John Webster — EMOTHE0147_TheWhiteDevil

Dramatis personae

  • MONTICELSO, a Cardinal; afterwards Pope PAUL IV
  • FRANCISCO DE MEDICIS, Duke of Florence; in the fifth act disguised for a Moor, under the name of MULINASSAR
  • BRACHIANO, otherwise PAULO GIORDANO URSINI, Duke of Brachiano; husband to Isabella and in love with Vittoria
  • GIOVANNI, his son, by Isabella
  • LODOVICO or LODOWICK, an Italian Count, but decayed
  • ANTONELLI
  • GASPARO
  • CAMILLO
  • HORTENSIO, one of Brachiano’s officers
  • MARCELLO, and attendant of the Duke of Florence, and brother to Vittoria
  • FLAMINEO, his brother; secretary to Brachiano
  • CARDINAL OF ARRAGON
  • DOCTOR JULIO, a conjuror
  • CHRISTOPHERO, his assistant
  • GUID-ANTONIO
  • FERENZE
  • JAQUES, a Moor, servant to Giovanni
  • ISABELLA, sister to Francisco de Medicis, and wife to Brachiano
  • VITTORIA COROMBONA, a Venetian lady, first married to Camillo, afterwards to Brachiano
  • CORNELIA, mother to Vittoria, Flamineo and Marcello
  • ZANCHE, a Moor; servant to Vittoria
  • MATRONA, of the House of Convertites
  • AMBASSADORS
  • PHYSICIANS
  • COURTIERS
  • LAWYERS
  • OFFICERS
  • ATTENDANTS
  • CHANCELLOR
  • REGISTRER
  • PAGE
  • ARMOURER
  • CONJUROR

[Act I, Scene i]

Enter Count LODOVICO, ANTONELLI and GASPARO

LODOVICO

1Banish’d?

ANTONELLI

2It griev’d me much to hear the sentence.

LODOVICO

3Ha, ha, O Democritus thy gods
4That govern the whole world! Fortune’s a right whore.
5If she gives ought, she deals it in small parcels.
6That she may take away all at one swoop.
7This ‘tis to have great enemies, God quite them:
8Your wolf no longer seems to be a wolf
9That when she’s hungry.

GASPARO

10Are men of princely rank

LODOVICO

11Oh I pray for them.
12The violent thunder is adored by those
13Are pash’d in pieces by it.

ANTONELLI

14You are justly doom’d; look but a little back
15Into yout former life: you have in three years
16Ruin’d the noblest cardiom –

GASPARO

17Your followers
18Have swallowed you like mummia, and being sick
19With such unnatural and horrid physic
20Vomit you up I’th’ kennel –

ANTONELLI

21All the damnable degrees
22Of drinkings have you stagger’d through; one citizen
23Is lord of two fair manors, call’d you master
24Only for caviare.

GASPARO

Only for caviare. Those noblemen
25Which were invited to your prodigal feasts,
26Wherein the phoenix scarce could scape your throats,
27Laugh at your misery, as fore deeming you
28An idle meteor which drawn forth the earth
29Would be soon lost I’th’air.

ANTONELLI

Would be soon lost I’th’air. Jest upon you,
30And say you were begotten in an earthquake,
31You have ruin’d such fair lordships.

LODOVICO

You have ruin’d such fair lordships. Very good,
32This well goes with two buckets, I must tend
33The pouring out of either.

GASPARO

The pouring out of either. Worse than these,
34You have acted certain murders here in Rome,
35Bloody and full of horror.

LODOVICO

Bloody and full of horror. ‘Las they were flea-bitings:
36Why took they not my head then?

GASPARO

Why took they not my head then? O my lord
37The law doth sometimes mediate, thinks it good
38Not ever to steep violent sins in blood;
39This gentle penance may both en your crimes,
40And in the example better these bad times.

LODOVICO

41So; but I wonder then some great men scape
42This banishment; there’s Paulo Giordano Orsini,
43The Duke of Brachiano, now lives in Rome,
44And by close panderism seeks to prostitute
45The honour of Vittoria Corombona:
46Vittoria, she that might have got my pardon
47For one kiss to the Duke.

ANTONELLI

48Have a full man within you.
49We see that trees bear no such pleasant fruit
50There where they grew first, as where they are new set.
51Perfumes the more they are chaf’d the more they render
52Their pleasing scents, and so affliction
53Expresseth virtue, fully, whether true,
54Or else adulterate.

LODOVICO

Or else adulterate. Leave your painted conforts.
55I’ll make Italian cut-works in their guts
56If ever I return.

GASPARO

If ever I return. O sir.

LODOVICO

If ever I return. O sir. I am patient.
57I have seen some ready to be executed
58Give pleasant looks, and money, and grown familiar
59With the knave hangman; so do I, I thank them,
60And would account them nobly merciful
61Would they dispatch me quickly.

ANTONELLI

Would they dispatch me quickly. Fare you well,
62We shall find time I doubt not, to repeal
63[A sennet sounds.] Your banishment.

LODOVICO

[A sennet sounds.] Your banishment. I am ever bound to you;
64This is the world’s alms; pray make use of it:
65Great men sell sheep, thus to be cut in pieces,
66When first they have shorn them bare and sold their fleeces.

Exeunt

[Act I, Scene ii]

Enter BRACHIANO, CAMILLO, FLAMINEO, VITTORIA, CORMBONA [and ATTENDANTS]

BRACHIANO

1Your best of rest.

VITTORIA

Your best of rest. Unto my lord the Duke,
2The best of welcome. More lights, attend the Duke.

[Exeunt VITTORIA and CAMILLO]

BRACHIANO

3Flamineo.

FLAMINEO

Flamineo. My lord.

BRACHIANO

Flamineo. My lord. Quite lost Flamineo.

FLAMINEO

4Pursue your noble wishes. I am promt
5As lightning to your service, O my lord!
6(whispers) The fair Vittoria, my happy sister
7Shall give you present audience. Gentelmen
8Let the caroche go on, and ‘tis his pleasure
9You put out all your torches and depart.

[Exeunt ATTENDANTS]

BRACHIANO

10Are we so happy?

FLAMINEO

Are we so happy? Can’t be otherwise?
11Observ’d you not tonight my honour’d lord,
12Wich way so e’er you went she threw her eyes?
13I have dealt already with her chamber-maid
14Zanche the Moor, and she is wondrous proud
15To be the agent for so high a spirit.

BRACHIANO

16We are happy above thought, because ‘bove merit.

FLAMINEO

17‘Bove merit! We may now talk freely: ‘bove merit; what is’t
18you doubt? Her coyness? That’s but the superficies of lust
19most women have; yet why should ladies blush to hear that
20nam’d, which they do not fear to handle? O they are politic!
21They know our desire is increas’d by the difficulty of
22enjoying; whereas satiety is a blunt, weary and drowsy
23passion; if the buttery-hatch at court stood continually
24open there would be nothing so passionate crowding, nor
25hot suit after the brevage,—

BRACHIANO

hot suit after the brevage,— O but her jealous husband.

FLAMINEO

26Hang him, a gilder that hath his brains perish’d with
27Quicksilver is not more cold in the liver. The great barriers
28moulted not more feathers than he hath shed hairs, by the
29confession of his doctor. An Irish gamester that will play
30himself nacked, and then wage all downward, at hazard, is
31not more venturous. So unable to please a woman that
32like a Dutch doublet all his back is shrunk into his breeches.
33Shroud you within this closet, good my lord;
34Some trick now must be thought in to divide
35My brother-in-law from his fair bed-fellow.

BRACHIANO

36O should she fail to come, —

FLAMINEO

37I must not have your lordship thus unwisely amorous; I
38myself have loved a lady and pursued her with a great deal
39of under-age protestation, whom some 3 or 4 gallants that
40have been rid of. ‘Tis just like a summer bird-cage in a
41garden: the birds that are within despair and are in a consumption
42for fear they shall never get out. Away, away my lord,

Enter CAMILLO

43See, here he comes.

[Exit BRACHIANO;]

44[FLAMINEO speaks aside to this fellow by his apparel.] Some men would judge a politician,
45But call his wit in question you shall find it
46[To CAMILLO] How now, brother,
47Merely an ass in’s foot-cloth.
48What, travelling to bed to your kind wife?

CAMILLO

49I assure you brother, no. My voyage lies
50More northerly, in a far colder clime;
51I do not well remember, I protest,
52When I last lay with her.

FLAMINEO

When I last lay with her. Strange you should lose your count.

CAMILLO

53We never lay together bur ere morning
54There grew a flaw between us.

FLAMINEO

There grew a flaw between us. ‘T had been your part
55To have made up that flaw.

CAMILLO

To have made up that flaw. True, but she loathes
56I should be seen in’t.

FLAMINEO

I should be seen in’t. Why sir, what’s the matter?

CAMILLO

57The Duke your master visits me, I thank him,
58And I perceive how like an earnest bowler
59He very passionately leans that way,
60He should have his bowl run.

FLAMINEO

He should have his bowl run. I hope you do not think —

CAMILLO

61That noblemen bowl booty? ‘Faith his cheek
62Hath a most excellent bias; it would fain
63Jump with my mistress.

FLAMINEO

Jump with my mistress. Will you be an ass
64Despite your Aristotle or a cuckold
65Contrary to your ephemerides
66Wich shows you under what a smiling planet
67You were first swaddled?

CAMILLO

You were first swaddled? Per wew, sir tell not me
68Of planets nor of ephemerides.
69A man may be made cuckold in the day-time
70When the stars’ eyes are out.

FLAMINEO

When the stars’ eyes are out. Sir God boy you,
71I do commit you to your pitiful pillow
72Stuff’d with horn-shavings.

CAMILLO

Stuff’d with horn-shavings. Brother?

FLAMINEO

Stuff’d with horn-shavings. Brother? God refuse me,
73Might I advise you now your only course
74Were to lock up your wife.

CAMILLO

Were to lock up your wife. ‘Twere very good.

FLAMINEO

75Bar her the sight of revels.

CAMILLO

Bar her the sight of revels. Excellent.

FLAMINEO

76Let her not go to church, but like a hound
77In leon at your heels.

CAMILLO

In leon at your heels. ‘Twere for her honour.

FLAMINEO

78And so you should be certain in one fortnight,
79Despite her chastity or innocence
80To be cuckolded, which yet is in suspense:
81This is my counsel and I ask no fee for’t.

CAMILLO

82Come, you know not where my nightcap wrings me.

FLAMINEO

83Wear it o’th’ old fashion, let your large ears come through, it will be more easy; nay, I will be bitter; bar your wife of her entertainment: women are more willingly and more gloriously chaste, when they are least restrained of their liberty. It seems you would be a fine capricious mathematically jealous coxcomb, take the height of your own horns with a Jacob’s staff afore they are up. These politic enclosures for paltry mutton makes more rebellion in the flesh than all the provocative electuaries doctors have uttered since last Jubilee.

CAMILLO

84This does not physic me.

FLAMINEO

85It seems you are jealous. I’ll show you the error of it by a familiar example: I have seen a pair of spectacles fashion’d with such perspective art, that lay down but one twelve pence o’th’ board, ‘twill appear as if there were twenty; now should you wear a pair of these spectacles, and see your wife tying her shoe, you would imagine twenty hands were taking up of your wife’s clothes, and this would put you into a horrible causeless fury.

CAMILLO

86The fault there sir is not in the eyesight—

FLAMINEO

87Enter [VITTORIA] COROMBONA True, but they that have the yellow jaundice, think all objects they look on to be yellow. Jealousy is worser, her fits present to a man, like so many bubbles in a basin of water, twenty several crabbed faces; many times majes his own shadow his cuckold-maker. [aside to VITTORIA] my lord attends you in the banqueting-house your husband is wondrous discontented. 88See she comes; what reason have you to be jealous of this creature? What an ignorant ass or flattering knave might he be counted, that should write sonnets to her eyes, or call her brow the snow of Ida, or ivory of Cornith, or compare her hair to the blackbird’s bill, when ‘tis liker the black- bird’s feather. This is all. Be wise; I will make you, it shall not be your seeking, do you stand upon that by any means; walk you aloof, I would not have you seen in’t. Sister,

VITTORIA

89I did nothing to displease him, I carved to him at supper-time.

FLAMINEO

90[aside to VITTORIA] You need not have carved him in faith, they say he is a capon already. I must now seemingly fall out with you. –Shall a gentleman so well descended as Camillo- a lousy slave that within this twenty years rode with the black-guard in the Duke’s carriage ‘mongst spits and dripping-pans,—

CAMILLO

91Now he benigs to tickle her.

FLAMINEO

92An excellent scholar, -one that hath a head fill’d with calves’ brains without any sage in them,-come crouching in the hams to you for a night’s lodging-that hath an itch in’s hams, which like the fire at the glass-house hath not gone out this seven years.-Is he not a courtly gentleman?- When he wears white stain one would take him by his black muzzle to be no other creature than a maggot.-You are a goodly foil, I confess, well set out-but cover’d with a false stone yon counterfeit diamond.

CAMILLO

93He will make her know what is in me.

FLAMINEO

94Come, my lord attends you; thou shalt go to bed to my lord.

CAMILLO

95Now he comes to’t.

FLAMINEO

96With a relish as curious as a vintner going to taste new wine. [To CAMILLO] I am opening you case hard.

CAMILLO

97A virtuous brother, o’ my credit.

FLAMINEO

98He will give thee a ring with a philosopher’s stone in it.

CAMILLO

99Indeed I am studying alchemy.

FLAMINEO

100Thou shalt lie in a bed stuff’d with turtles’ feathers, swoon in perfumed linen like the fellow was smothered in roses; so perfect shall be thy happiness, that as men at sea think land and trees and ships go that way they go, so both heaven and earth shall seem to go your voyage. Shalt meet him, ‘tis fix’d, with nails of diamonds to inevitable necessity.

VITTORIA

101[aside to FLAMINEO] How shall’s rid him hence?

FLAMINEO

102I will put breese in’s tail, set him gadding presently. [To CAMILLO] I have almost wrought her to it, I find her coming, but might I advise you now for this night I would not lie with her; I would cross her humour to make her more humble.

CAMILLO

103Shall I? Shall I?

FLAMINEO

104It will show in you a supremacy of judgement.

CAMILLO

105True, and a mind differing from the tumultuary opinion, for quae negate grata.

FLAMINEO

106Right: you are the adamant shall draw her to you, though you keep distance off.

CAMILLO

107A philosophical reason.

FLAMINEO

108Walk by her o’ the nobleman’s fashion, and tell her you will lie with her at the end of the progress.

CAMILLO

109Vittoria, I cannot be induc’d or as a man would say incited—

VITTORIA

110To do what sir?

CAMILLO

111To lie with you tonight; your silkworm useth to fast everythird day, and the next following spins the better. Tomorrow at night I am for you.

VITTORIA

112You’ll spin a fair thread, trust to’t.

FLAMINEO

113But do you hear, I shall have you steal to her chamber about midnight.

CAMILLO

114Do you think so? Why look you brother, because you shall not think I’ll gull you, take the key, lock me into the chamber, and say you shall be sure of me.

FLAMINEO

115In troth I will, I’ll be your jailer once;
116But have you ne’er a false door?

CAMILLO

117A pox on’t, as I am a Christian tell me tomorrow how scurvily she takes my unkink parting.

FLAMINEO

118I will.

CAMILLO

119Didst thou not mark the jest of the silkworm?
120Good night: in faith I will use this trick often, —

Exit CAMILLO

FLAMINEO

121Do , do, do.
122So now you are safe. Ha ha ha, thou entanglest thyself

Enter BRACHIANO

123in thine own work like a silkworm.
124Come sister, darkness hides your blush; women are like
125curs’d dogs, civility keeps tied all daytime, but they
126are let loose at midnight; then they do most good or most
127mischief. My lord, my lord.

BRACHIANO

128Give credit: I could wish time would stand still
129And never end this interview, this hour,
130But all delight doth itself soon’st devour

ZANCHE brings out a carpet, spreads it and lays on it two fair cushions. Enter CORELLA [listening, behind].

131Let me into your bosom happy lady,
132Pour out instead of eloquence my vows;
133Loose me not madam, for it you forgo me
134I am lost eternally.

VITTORIA

I am lost eternally. Sir in the way of pity
135I wish you heart-whole.

BRACHIANO

I wish you heart-whole. You are a sweet physician.

VITTORIA

136Sure sir a loathed cruelty in ladies
137Is as to doctors many funerals.
138It takes away their credit.

BRACHIANO

It takes away their credit. Excellent creature.
139We call the cruel fair, what name for you
140That are so merciful?

[Embraces her]

ZANCHE

That are so merciful? See now they close.

FLAMINEO

That are so merciful? See now they close. Most happy union.

CORNELIA

141[aside] My fears are fall’n upon me, oh my heart!aparte
142My son the pander: now I find our house
143Sinking to ruin. Earthquakes leave behind,
144Where they have tyrannized, iron or lead, or stone,
145But, woe to ruin! Violent lust leaves none.

BRACHIANO

146What value is this jewel?

VITTORIA

What value is this jewel? 'Tis the ornament
147Of a weak fortune.

BRACHIANO

148In sooth I'll have it; nay I will but change
149My jewel for your jewel.

FLAMINEO

My jewel for your jewel. Excellent,
150His jewel for her jewel; well put in Duke.

BRACHIANO

151Nay let me see you wear it.

VITTORIA

Nay let me see you wear it. Here sir.

BRACHIANO

152Nay lower, you shall wear my jewel lower.

FLAMINEO

153That's better; she must wear his jewel lower.

VITTORIA

154To pass away the time I'll tell your grace
155A dream I had last night.

BRACHIANO

156Most wishedly.

VITTORIA

Most wishedly. A foolish idle dream:
157Methought I walk'd about the mid of night,
158Into a church-yard, where a goodly yew-tree
159Spread her large root in ground; under that yew,
160As I sat sadly leaning on a grave,
161Checkered with cross-sticks, there came stealling in
162Your Duchess and my husband; one of them
163A pick-axe bore, th'other a rusty spade,
164And in rough terms they gan to challenge me,
165About this yew.

BRACHIANO

About this yew. That tree.

VITTORIA

About this yew. That tree. This harmless yew.
166They told me my intent was to root up
167That well-grown yew, and plant i'th' stead of it
168A withered blackthorn, and for that they vow'd
169To bury me alive: my husband straigh
170With pick-axe gan to dig, and your fell Duchess
171With shovel, like a fury, voided out
172The earth and scattered bones. Lord how methought
173I trembled, and yet for all this terror
174I could not pray.

FLAMINEO

I could not pray. No the devil was in your dream.

VITTORIA

175When to my rescue there arose me thought
176A whirlwind, which let fall a massy arm
177From that strong plant,
178And both were struck dead by that scared yew
179In that base shallow grave that was their due.

FLAMINEO

180Excellent devil.
181She hath taught him in a dream
182To make away his Duchess and her husband.

BRACHIANO

183Sweetly shall I interpret this your dream.
184You are lodged within his arms who shall protect you,
185From all the fevers of a jealous husband,
186From the poor envy of our phlegmatic Duchess;
187I'll seat you above law and above scandal,
188Give to your thoughts the invention of delight
189And the fruition; nor shall government
190Divide me from you longer than a care
191To keep you great: you shall to me at once
192Be dukedom, health, wife, children friends and all.

CORNELIA

193[approaching them] Woe to light hearts, they still forerun our fall.

FLAMINEO

194What fury rais'd thee up? Away, away!

Exit ZANCHE

CORNELIA

195What make you here my lord this dead of night?
196Never dropp'd mildew on a flower here,
197Till now.

FLAMINEO

Till now. I pray you go to bed then,
198Lest you be blasted?

CORNELIA

Lest you be blasted? O that this fair garden,
199Had with all poison'd herbs of Thessaly,
200At first been planted, made a nursery
201For wichcraft; rather than a burial plot
202For both your honours.

VITTORIA

For both your honours. Dearest mother hear me.

CORNELIA

203O thou dost make my brow bend to the earth,
204Sooner than nature; see the curse of children:
205In life they keep us frequently in tears,
206And in the cold grave leave us in pale fears.

BRACHIANO

207Come, come , I will not hear you.

VITTORIA

Come, come , I will not hear you. Dear my lord.

CORNELIA

208Where is thy Duchess now adulterous Duke?
209Thou little dream'd'st this night she is come to Rome.

FLAMINEO

210How? Come to Rome, —

VITTORIA

How? Come to Rome, — The Duchess, —

BRACHIANO

How? Come to Rome, — The Duchess, — She had been better,—

CORNELIA

211The lives of princes should like dials move,
212Whose regular example is so strong,
213They make the times by them go right or wrong.

FLAMINEO

214So, have you done?

CORNELLIA

So, have you done? Unfortunate Camillo.

VITTORIA

215I do protest if any chaste denial,
216If anything but blood could have allayed
217His long suit to me —

CORNELLIA

His long suit to me — I will join with thee,
218To the most woeful end e'er mother kneel'd,
219If thou dishonour thus thy husband's bed,
220Be thy life short as are the funeral tears
221In great men's.

BRACHIANO

In great men's. Fie, fie, the woman's mad.

CORNELIA

222Be thy act Judas-like, betray in kissing;
223May'st thou be envied during his short breath,
224And pitied like a wretch after his death.

VITTORIA

225O me accurs'd.

Exit VITTORIA

FLAMINEO

O me accurs'd. Are you out of your wits, my lord?
226I'll fetch her back again.

BRACHIANO

I'll fetch her back again. No I'll to bed.
227Send Doctor Julio to me presently.
228Uncharitable woman, thy rash tongue
229Hath rais'd a fearful and prodigious storm,
230Be thou the cause of all ensuing harm.

Exit BRACHIANO

FLAMINEO

231Now, you that stand so much upon your honour,
232Is this a fitting time o' night think you,
233To send a duke home without e'er a man?
234I would fain know where lies the mass of wealth
235Which you have hoarded for my maintenance,
236That I may bear my beard out of the level
237Of my lord's stirrup.

CORNELIA

Of my lord's stirrup. What? Because we are poor
238Shall we be vicious?

FLAMINEO

Shall we be vicious? Pray what means have you
239To keep me from the galleys, or the gallows?
240My father prov'd himself a gentleman,
241Sold all's land, and like a fortunate fellow,
242Died ere the money was spent. You brought me up,
243At Padua I confess, where, I protest,
244For want of means, (the university judge me,)
245I have been fain to heel my tutor's stockings
246At least seven years. Conspiring with a beard
247Made me a graduate, then to this Duke's service;
248I visited the court, whence I return'd —
249More courteous, more lecherous by far,
250But not a suit the richer; and shall I,
251Having a path so open and so free
252To my preferment, still retain your milk
253In my pale forehead? No, this face of mine
254I'll arm and fortify with lusty wine
255'Gainst shame and blushing.

CORNELIA

256O that I ne'er had borne thee, —

FLAMINEO

O that I ne'er had borne thee, — So would I.
257I would the common'st courtezan in Rome
258Had been my mother rather than thyself.
259Nature is very pitiful to whores
260To give them but few children, yet those children
261Plurality of fathers; they are sure
262They shall not want. Go, go,
263Complain unto my great lord cardinal,
264Yet may be he will justify the act.
265Lycurgus wond'red much men would provide
266Good stallions for their mares, and yet would suffer
267Their fair wives to be barren, —

CORNELIA

Their fair wives to be barren, — Misery of miseries.

Exit CORNELIA

FLAMINEO

268The Duchess come to court? I like not that;
269We are engag'd to mischief and must on.
270As rivers to find out the ocean
271Flow with crook bendings beneath forced banks,
272Or as we see, to aspire some mountain's top
273The way ascends not straight, but imitates
274The subtle foldings of a winter's snake,
275So who knows policy and her true aspect,
276Shall find her ways winding and indirect.

Exit

[Act II, Scene i]

Enter FRANCISCO DE MEDICI, Cardinal MONTICELSO, MARCELLO, ISABELLA, young GIOVANNI, with little JAQUES the Moor

FRANCISCO

1Have you not seen your husband since you arrived?

ISABELLA

2Not yet sir.

FRANCISCO

Not yet sir. Surely he is wondrous kind.
3If I had such a dove house as Camillo's
4I would set fire on't, were't but to destroy
5The pole-cats that haunt to't, - my sweet cousin.

GIOVANNI

6Lord uncle you did promise me a horse
7And armour.

FRANCISCO

And armour. That I did my pretty cousin.
8Marcello see it fitted.

MARCELLO

Marcello see it fitted. My lord, the Duke is here.

FRANCISCO

9Sister away, you must not yet be seen.

ISABELLA

10I do beseech you
11Entreat him mildly, let not your rough tongue
12Set us at louder variance; all my wrongs
13Are freely pardoned, and I do not doubt
14As men to try the precious unicorn's horn
15Make of the powder a preservative circle
16And in it put a spider, so these arms
17Shall charm his poison, force it to obeying
18And keep him chaste from an infected straying.

FRANCISCO

19I wish I may. Be gone.

Exit [ISABELLA]

Enter BRACHIANO and FLAMINEO

I wish I may. Be gone. Void the chamber.

[Exeunt FLAMINEO, MARCELLO, GIOVANNI and JAQUES]

20You are welcome, will you sit? I pray my lord
21Be you my orator, my heart's too full;
22I'll second you anon.

MONTICELSO

I'll second you anon. Ere I begin
23Let me entreat your Grace forgo all passion
24Which may be raised by my free discourse.

BRACHIANO

25As silent as i'th' church – you may proceed

MONTICELSO

26It is a wonder to your noble friends,
27That you that have as 'twere ent'red the world,
28With a free sceptre in your able hand,
29And have to th'use of nature well applied
30High gifts of learning, should in your prime age
31Neglect your awful throne, for the soft down
32Of an insatiate bed. Oh my lord,
33The drunkard after all his lavish cups,
34Is dry, and then is sober; so at length,
35When you awake from this lascivious dream,
36Repentance then will follow; like the sting
37Plac'd in the adder's tail: wretched are princes
38When fortune blasteth but a petty flower
39Of their unwiedly crowns; or ravisheth
40But one pearl from their sceptre: but alas!
41When they to wilful shipreck loose good frame
42All princely titles perish with their name.

BRACHIANO

43You have said my lord, –

MONTICELSO

You have said my lord, – Enough to give you taste
44How far I am from flattering your greatness?

BRACHIANO

45Now you that are his second, what say you?
46Do not like young hawks fetch a course about;
47Your game flies fair and for you, –

FRANCISCO

Your game flies fair and for you, – Do not fear it:
48I'll answer you in your own hawking phrase.
49Some eagles that should gaze upon the sun
50Seldom soar high, but take their lustful ease
51Since they from dunghill birds their prey can seize.
52You know Vittoria?

BRACHIANO

You know Vittoria? Yes.

FRANCISCO

You know Vittoria? Yes. You shift your shirt there
53When you retire from tennis.

BRACHIANO

When you retire from tennis. Happily.

FRANCISCO

54Her husband is lord of a poor fortune
55Yet she wears cloth of tissue, –

BRACHIANO

Yet she wears cloth of tissue, – What of this?
56Will you urge that my good lord cardinal
57As part of her confession at next shrift,
58And know from whence it sails?

FRANCISCO

And know from whence it sails? She is your strumpet, –

BRACHIANO

59Uncivil sir there's hemlock in thy breath
60And that black slander; were she a whore of mine
61All thy loud cannons, and thy borrowed Switzers
62Thy galleys, nor thy sworn confederates
63Durst not supplant her.

FRANCISCO

Durst not supplant her. Let's not talk on thunder.
64Thou hast a wife, our sister; would I had given
65Both her white hands to death, bound and lock'd fast
66In her last winding-sheet, when I gave thee
67But one.

BRACHIANO

But one. Thou hadst given a soul to God then.

FRANCISCO

But one. Thou hadst given a soul to God then. True:
68Thy ghostly father with all's absolution,
69Shall ne'er do so by thee.

BRACHIANO

Shall ne'er do so by thee. Spit thy poison, –

FRANCISCO

70I shall not need, lust carries her sharp whip
71At her own girdle; look to't for our anger
72Is making thunder-bolts.

BRACHIANO

Is making thunder-bolts. Thunder? in faith,
73They are but crackers.

FRANCISCO

They are but crackers. We'll end this with the cannon.

BRACHIANO

74Thou'lt get nought by it but iron in thy wounds,
75And gunpowder in thy nostrils.

FRANCISCO

And gunpowder in thy nostrils. Better that
76Than change perfumes for plasters, –

BRACHIANO

Than change perfumes for plasters, – Pity on thee,
77'Twere good you'ld show your slaves or men condemn'd
78Your new-plough'd forehead. Defiance!-and I'll meet thee,
79Even in a thicket of thy ablest men.

MONTICELSO

80My lords, you shall not word it any further
81Without a milder limit.

FRANCISCO

Without a milder limit. Willingly.

BRACHIANO

82Have you proclaimed a triumph that you bait
83A lion thus?

MONTICELSO

A lion thus? My lord.

BRACHIANO

A lion thus? My lord. I am tame sir.

FRANCISCO

84We send unto the Duke for conference
85'Bout levies 'gainst the pirates; my lord Duke
86Is not at home; we come ourself in person,
87Still my lord Duke is busied; but we fear
88Discovers flocks of wild ducks, then my lord
89('Bout moulting time I mean,) we shall be certain
90To find you sure enough and speak with you.

BRACHIANO

To find you sure enough and speak with you. Ha?

FRANCISCO

91A mere tale of a tub, my words are idle,
92But to express the sonnet by natural reason,
93When stags grow melancholic you'll find the season –

Enter GIOVANNI

MONTICELSO

94No more my lord; here comes a champion,
95Shall end the difference between you both,
96Your son the prince Giovanni. See my lords
97What hopes you store in him; this is a casket
98For both your crowns, and should be held like clear:
99Now is he apt for knowledge; therefore know
100It is a more direct and even way
101To train to virtue those of princely blood
102By examples than by precepts: if by examples
103Whom should he rather strive to imitate
104Than his own father? Be his pattern then,
105Leave him a stock of virtue that may last,
106Should fortune rend his sails, and split his mast.

BRACHIANO

107Your hand boy-growing to a soldier?

GIOVANI

Your hand boy-growing to a soldier? Give me a pike.

FRANCISCO

108What, practising your pike so young, fair coz?

GIOVANNI

109Suppose me one of Homer's frogs, my lord,
110Tossing my bullrush thus. Pray sir tell me
111Might not a child of good discretion
112Be leader to an army?

FRANCISCO

Be leader to an army? Yes cousin, a young prince
113Of good discretion might.

GIOVANNI

Of good discretion might. Say you so?
114Indeed I have head 'tis fit a general
115Should not endanger his own person oft,
116So that he make a noise, when he's horseback
117Like a Dansk drummer. O 'tis excellent!
118He need not fight; methinks his horse as well
119Might lead an army for him; if I live
120I'll challenge the French foe, in the very front
121Of all my troops, the foremost man.

FRANCISCO

Of all my troops, the foremost man. What, what, –

GIOVANNI

122And will not bid my soldiers up and follow
123But bid them follow me.

BRACHIANO

But bid them follow me. Forward lapwing.
124He files with the shell on's head.

FRANCISCO

He files with the shell on's head. Pretty cousin.

GIOVANNI

125The first year uncle that I go to war
126All prisoners that I take I will set free
127Without their ransome.

FRANCISCO

Without their ransome. Ha, without their ransome?
128That took those prisoners for you?

GIOVANNI

That took those prisoners for you? Thus my lord:
129I'll marry them to all the wealthy windows
130That falls that year.

FRANCISCO

That falls that year. Why then the next year following
131You'll have no men to go with you to war.

GIOVANNI

132Why then I'll press the women to the war,
133And then the men will follow.

MONTICELSO

And then the men will follow. Witty prince.

FRANCISCO

134See a good habit makes a child a man,
135Whereas a bad one makes a man a beast:
136Come, you and I are friends.

BRACHIANO

Come, you and I are friends. Most wishedly;
137Like bones which broke in sunder and well set
138Knit the more strongly.

FRANCISCO

Knit the more strongly. [calls offstage] Call Camillo hither.
139You have received the rumour, how Count Lodowick
140Is turn'd a pirate?

BRACHIANO

Is turn'd a pirate? Yes.

FRANCISCO

Is turn'd a pirate? Yes. We are now preparing
141Some ships to fetch him in.

[Enter ISABELLA]

142Behold your Duchess;
143We now will leave you and expect from you
144Nothing but kind entreaty.

BRACHIANO

Nothing but kind entreaty. You have charm'd me.

Exeunt FR[ANCISCO], MON[TICELSO], GIOV[ANNI]

145You are in health we see.

ISABELLA

You are in health we see. And above health
146To see my lord well.

BRACHIANO

To see my lord well. So I wonder much,
147What amorous whirlwind hurried you to Rome –

ISABELLA

148Devotion my lord.

BRACHIANO

Devotion my lord. Devotion?
149Is your soul charg'd with a grievous sin?

ISABELLA

150'Tis burdened with too many, and I think
151The oft'ner that we cast our reck'nings up,
152Our sleeps will be the sounder.

BRACHIANO

Our sleeps will be the sounder. Take your chamber.

ISABELLA

153Nay my dear lord, I will not have you angry;
154Doth not my absence from you two months
155Merit one kiss?

BRACHIANO

Merit one kiss? I do not use to kiss.
156If that will dispossess your jealousy,
157I'll swear it to you.

ISABELLA

I'll swear it to you. O my loved lord,
158I do not come to chide; my jealousy?
159I am to learn what that Italian means;
160You are as welcome to these longing arms,
161As I to you a virgin.

[She tries to embrace him; he turns away]

BRACHIANO

As I to you a virgin. O your breath!
162Out upon sweetmeats, and continued physic!
163The plague is in them.

ISABELLA

The plague is in them. You have oft for these two lips
164Neglected cassia or the natural sweets
165Of the spring violet; they are not yet much withered.
166My lord I should be merry; these your frowns
167Show in a helmet lovely, but on me,
168In such a peaceful interview methinks
169They are too roughly knit.

BRACHIANO

They are too roughly knit. O dissemblance!
170Do you bandy factions 'ganst me? Have you learnt
171The trick of imprudent baseness to complain
172Unto your kindred?

ISABELLA

Unto your kindred? Never my dear lord.

BRACHIANO

173Must I be haunted out, or was't your trick
174To meet some amorous gallant here ir Rome
175That must supply our discontinuance?

ISABELLA

176I pray sir burst my heart, and in my death
177Turn to your ancient pity, though not love.

BRACHIANO

178Beacuse your brother is the corpulent Duke,
179That is the great Duke, -'Sdeath I shall not shortly
180Racket away five hundred crowns at tennis,
181But it shall rest upon record. I scorn him
182Like a shav'd Polack; all his reverent wit
183Lies in his wardrobe; he's a discreet fellow
184When he's made up in his robes of state, –
185Your brother the great Duke, because h'as galleys,
186And now and then ransacks a Turkish fly-boat,
187(Now all the hellish Furies take his soul,)
188First made this match, -accursed be the priest
189That sang the wedding mass, and even my issue.

ISABELLA

190O too, too far you have curs'd.

BRACHIANO

O too, too far you have curs'd. Your hand I'll kiss:
191This is the latest ceremony of my love,
192Henceforth I'll never lie with thee, by this,
193This wedding ring: I'll ne'er more lie with thee.
194And this divorce shall be as truly kept,
195A if the judge had doom'd it: fare you well,
196Our sleeps are sever'd.

ISABELLA

Our sleeps are sever'd. Forbid it the sweet union
197Of all things blessed; why the saints in heaven
198Will knit their brows at that.

BRACHIANO

Will knit their brows at that. Let not thy love
199Shall never on my soul be satisfied
200With my repentance: let thy brother rage
201Beyond a horrid tempest or sea-fight,
202My vow is fixed.

ISABELLA

My vow is fixed. O my winding sheet,
203Now shall I need thee shortly. Dear my lord,
204Let me hear once more what I would not hear:
Let me hear once more what I would not hear: Never?

BRACHIANO

Let me hear once more what I would not hear: Never? Never!

ISABELLA

205O my unkind lord may your sins find mercy,
206As I upon a woeful widowed bed
207Shall pray for you, if not to turn your eyes
208Upon your wretched wife, and hope son,
209Yet that in time you'll fix them upon heaven.

BRACHIANO

210No more; go, go complain to the great Duke.

ISABELLA

211No my dear lord, you shall have present witness
212How I'll work peace between you; I will make
213Myself the author of your cursed vow.
214I have some cause to do it, you have none;
215Conceal it I beseech you, for the weal
216Of both your dukedoms, that you wrought the means
217Of such a separation; let the fault
218Remain with my supposed jealousy,
219And think with what a piteous and rent heart
220I shall perform this sad ensuing part.

Enter FRANCISCO, FLAMINEO, MONTICELSO; MARCELLO

BRACHIANO

221Well, take your course; my honourable brother!

FRANCISCO

222Sister! -this is not well my lord,- why sister!
223She merits not this welcome.

BRACHIANO

She merits not this welcome. Welcome, say?
224She hath given a sharp welcome.

FRANCISCO

She hath given a sharp welcome. Are you foolish?
225Come dry your tears; is this a modest course?
226To better what is nought, to rail, and weep?
227Grow to a reconcilement, or by heaven,
228I'll ne'er more deal between you.

ISABELLA

I'll ne'er more deal between you. Sir you shall not,
229No though Vittoria upon that condition
230Would become honest.

FRANCISCO

Would become honest. Was your husband loud,
231Since we departed?

ISABELLA

Since we departed? By my life sir no.
232I swear by that I do not care to lose.
233Are all these ruins of my former beauty
234Laid out for a whore's triumph?

FRANCISCO

Laid out for a whore's triumph? Do you hear?
235Look upon other women, with what patience
236They suffer these slight wrongs, with what justice
237They study to requite them; take that course.

ISABELLA

238O that I were a man, or that I had power
239To execute my apprehended wishes,
240I would whip some with scorpions.

FRANCISCO

I would whip some with scorpions. What? turn'd fury?

ISABELLA

241To dig the strumpet's eyes out, let her lie
242Some twenty months a-dying, to cut off
243Her nose and lips, pull out her rotten teeth,
244Preserve her flesh like mummia, for trophies
245Of my just anger. Hell to my affliction
246Is mere snow-water: by your favour sir, –
247Brother draw near, and my lord cardinal, –
248Sir let me borrow of you but one kiss,
249Henceforth I'll never lie with you, by this,
250This wedding-ring.

FRANCISCO

This wedding-ring. How? Ne'er more lie with him?
251And this divorce shall be as truly kept,
252As if in thronged court, a thousand ears
253Had heard it, and a thousand lawyers' hands
254Seal'd to the separation.

BRACHIANO

Seal'd to the separation. Ne'er lie with me?

ISABELLA

Seal'd to the separation. Ne'er lie with me? Let not my former dotage
255Make thee an unbeliever; this my vow
256Shall never on my soul be satisfied
257With my repentance: manet alta mente repostum.

FRANCISCO

258Was this your circle of pure unicorn's horn,
259You said should charm your lord? Now horn upon thee,
260For jealousy deserves them; keep your vow,
261And take your chamber.

ISABELLA

And take your chamber. No sir I'll presently to Padua,
262I will not stay a minute.

MONTICELSO

I will not stay a minute. O good madam.

BRACHIANO

263'Twere best to let her have her humour,
264Some half-day's journey will bring down her stomach,
265And then she'll turn in post.

FRANCISCO

And then she'll turn in post. To see her come
266To my lord cardinal for a dispensation
267Of her rash vow will beget excellent laughter.

ISABELLA

268Unkindness do thy office, poor hear break,
269Those are the killing griefs which dare not speak.

Exit

Enter CAMILLO

MARCELLO

270Camillo's come my lord.

FRANCISCO

Camillo's come my lord. Where's the commission?

MARCELLO

271'Tis here.

FRANCISCO

'Tis here. Give me the signet.

FLAMINEO

272[to BRACHIANO] My lord do you mark their whispering; I will compound a medicine out of their two heads, stronger than garlic, deadlier than stibium; the cantharides which are scarce seen to stick upon the flesh when they work to the heart, shall not do it with more silence or invisible cunning.

Enter Doctor [JULIO]

BRACHIANO

273About the murder.

FLAMINEO

274They are sending him to Naples, but I'll send him to Candy; here's another property too.

BRACHIANO

275O the doctor, –

FLAMINEO

276A poor quack-salving knave, my lord, one that should have been lash'd for's lechery, but that he confess'd a judgement, had an execution laid upon him, and so put the whip to a non plus.

DOCTOR

277And was cozen'd, my lord, by an arranter knave than myself, and made pay all the colourable execution.

FLAMINEO

278He will shoot pills into a man's guts, shall make them have more ventages than a cornet or a lamprey; he will poison a kiss, and was once minded, for his masterpiece, because Ireland breeds no poison, to have prepared a deadly vapour in a Spaniard's fart that should have posion'd all Dublin.

BRACHIANO

279O Saint Anthony's fire!

DOCTOR

280Your secretary in merry my lord.

FLAMINEO

281O thou cursed antipathy to nature! Look his eye's bloodshed like a needle a chirurgeon stitcheth a wound with. Let me embrace thee toad, and love thee, O thou abhominable loathsome gargarism, that will fetch up lungs, lights, heart, and liver by scrupules.

BRACHIANO

282No more; I must employ thee honest doctor,
283You must to Padua and by the way,
284Use some of your skill for us.

DOCTOR

Use some of your skill for us. Sir I shall.

BRACHIANO

285But for Camillo?

FLAMINEO

286He dies this night by such a politic strain,
287Men shall suppose him by's own engine slain.
288But for your Duchess' death?

DOCTOR

But for your Duchess' death? I'll make her sure.

BRACHIANO

289Small mischiefs are by greater made secure.

FLAMINEO

290Remember this you slave; when knaves come to preferment
291they rise as gallowses are raised i'th' Low Countries: one
292upon another's shoulders .

Exeunt [BRACHIANO, FLAMINEO and Doctor JULIO]

MONTICELSO

293Here is an emblem nephew, pray persuse it.
294'Twas thrown in at your window, –

CAMILLO

'Twas thrown in at your window, – At my window?
295Here ir a stag my lord hath shed his horns,
296And fot the loss of them the poor beast weeps.
297The word Inopem me copia fecit.

MONTICELSO

The word Inopem me copia fecit. That is:
298Plenty of horns hath made him poor of horns.

CAMILLO

299What should this mean?

MONTICELSO

What should this mean? I'll tell you: 'tis given out
300You are a cuckold.

CAMILLO

You are a cuckold. Is it given out so?
301I had rather such report as that my lord,
302Should keep within doors.

FRANCISCO

Should keep within doors. You are the happier:
303I'll tell you a tale.

CAMILLO

I'll tell you a tale. Pray my lord.

FRANCISCO

I'll tell you a tale. Pray my lord. An old tale.
304Upon a time Phoebus the god of light,
305Or him we call the sun, would need be married.
306The goods gave their consent, and Mercury
307Was sent to voice it to the general world.
308But what a piteous cry there straight arose
309Amongst smiths, and feltmakers, brewers and cooks,
310Reapers and butter-women, amongst fishmongers
311And thousand other trades, which are annoyed
312By his excessive heat; 'twas lamentable.
313They came to Jupiter all in a sweat
314And do forbid the bans; a great fat cook
315Was made their speaker, who entreats of Jove
316That Phoebus might be gelded, for if now
317When there was but one sun, so many men
318Were like to perish by his violent heat,
319What should they do if he were married
320And should beget more, and those children
321Make fireworks like their father? So say I,
322Only I will apply it to your wife:
323Her issue, should not providence prevent it,
324Would make both nature, time, and man repent it.

MONTICELSO

325Look you cousin,
326Go change the air for shame; see if your absence
327Will blast your cornucopia; Marcello
328Is chosen with you joint commissioner
329For the relieving our Italian coast
330From pirates.

MARCELLO

From pirates. I am much honour'd in't.

CAMILLO

From pirates. I am much honour'd in't. But sir
331Ere I return the stag's horns may be sprouted,
332Greater than these are shed.

MONTICELSO

Greater than these are shed. Do not fear it,
333I'll be your ranger.

CAMILLO

I'll be your ranger. You must watch i'th' nights,
334Then's the most danger.

FRANCISCO

Then's the most danger. Farewell good Marcello.
335All the best fortunes of a soldier's wish
336Bring you o' ship-board.

CAMILLO

337Were I not best now I am turn'd soldier,
338Ere than I leave my wife, sell all she hath
339And then take leave of her.

MONTICELSO

And then take leave of her. I expect good from you,
340Your parting is so merry.

CAMILLO

341Merry my lord, o'th' capitain's humour right;
342I am resolved to be drunk this night.

Exit [CAMILLO; with MARCELLO]

FRANCISCO

343So, 'twas well fitted: now shall we discern
344How his wish'd absence will give violent way
345To Duke Brachiano's lust, –

MONTICELSO

To Duke Brachiano's lust, – Why that was it;
346To what scorn'd purpose else should we make choice
347Of him for a sea-capiain, and besides,
348Count Lodowick which was rumour'd for a pirate,
349Is now in Padua.

FRANCISCO

Is now in Padua. It's true?

MONTICELSO

Is now in Padua. It's true? Most certain.
350I have letters from him, which are suppliant
351To work his quick repeal from banishment;
352He means to address himself for pension
353Unto our sister Duchess.

FRANCISCO

Unto our sister Duchess. O'twas well.
354We shall not want his absence past six days;
355I fain would have the Duke Brachiano run
356Into notorious scandal, for there's nought
357In such curs'd dotage, to repair his name,
358Only the deep sense of some deathless shame.

MONTICELSO

359It may be objected I am dishonourable,
360To play thus with my kinsman, but I answer,
361For my revenge I'd stake a brother's life,
362That being wrong'd durst not avenge himself.

FRANCISCO

363Come to observe this stumpet.

MONTICELSO

Come to observe this stumpet. Curse of greatness,
364Sure he'll not leave her.

FRANCISCO

Sure he'll not leave her. There's small pity in't.
365Like mistletoe on sere elms spent by weather,
366Let him cleave to her and both rot together.

Exeunt

[Act II, Scene ii]

Enter BRACHIANO with one in the habit of a Conjuror

BRACHIANO

1Now sir I claim your promise; 'tis dead midnight,
2The time prefix'd to show me by your art
3How the intended murder of Camillo,
4And our loathed Duchess grow to action.

CONJUROR

5You have won me by your bounty to a deed
6I do not often practise; some there are,
7Which by sophistic tricks, aspire that name
8Which I would glady lose, of nigromancer;
9As some that use to juggle upon cards,
10Seeming to conjure, when indeed they cheat;
11Others that raise up their confederate spirits,
12'Bout windmills, and endanger their own necks,
13For making of a squib; and some there are
14Will keep a curtal to show juggling tricks
15And give out 'tis a spirit: and some there are
16Will keep a curtal to show juggling tricks
17And give out 'tis a spirit: besides these
18Such a whole ream of almanac-makers, figure-flingers,
19Fellows indeed that only live by stealth,
20Since they do merely lie about stol'n goods,
21They'd make men think the devil were fast an loose,
22With speaking fustian Latin. Pray sit down,
23Put on this night-cap sir, 'tis charm'd, and now
24I'll show you by my strong-commanding art
25The circumstance that breaks your Duchess' heart.

A DUMB SHOW

Enter suspiciously, JULIO and CHRISTOPHERO; they draw a curtain where BRACHIANO's picture is, they put in spectacles of glass which cover their eyes and noses, and then burn perfumes afore the picture, and wash the lips of the picture; that done, quenching the fire, and putting off their spectacles off their depart laughing.

Enter ISABELLA in her nightgown as to bedward, with lights after her, Count LODOVICO, GIOVANNI, GUID-ANTONIO and others waiting on her; she kneels down as to prayers, then draws the curtain of the picture, does three reverences to it, and kisses thrice, she faints and will not suffer them to come near it, dies; sorrow express'd in GIOVANNI and in Count LODOVICO; she's convey'd out solemny.

BRACHIANO

26Excellent, then she's dead, –

CONJUROR

Excellent, then she's dead, – She's poisoned,
27By the fum'd picture: 'twas her custom nightly,
28Before she went to bed, to go and visit
29Your picture, and to fed her eyes and lips
30On the dead shadow; Doctor Julio
31Observing this, infects it with an oil
32And other poison’d stuff, which presently
33Did suffocate her spirits.

BRACHIANO

Did suffocate her spirits. Methought I saw
34Count Lodowick there.

CONJUROR

Count Lodowick there. He was, and by my art
35I find he did most passionately dote
36Upon your Duchess. Now turn another way,
37And view Camillo’s far more politic fate:
38Strike louder music from this charmed ground,
39To yield, as fits the act, a tragic sound.

THE SECOND DUMB SHOW

Enter FLAMINEO, MARCELLO, CAMILLO with four more as Capitains, they drink healths and dance; a vaulting-horse is brought into the room, MARCELLO and two more whisper’d out of the room, while FLAMINEO and CAMILLO strip themselves into their shirts, as to vault; compliment who shall begin, as CAMILLO is about to vault, FLAMINEO pitcheth him upon his neck, and with the help of the rest, writhes his neck about, seems to see if it be broke, and lays him folded double as ‘twere under the horse, makes shows to call for help, MARCELLO comes in, laments, sends for the Cardinal and Duke, who comes forth with armed men, wonder at the act; commands the body to be carried home, apprehends FLAMINEO, MARCELLO, and the rest, and go as ‘twere to apprehend VITTORIA.

BRACHIANO

40‘Twas quaintly done, but yet each circumstance
41I taste not fully.

CONJUROR

I taste not fully. O ‘twas most apparent,
42You saw them enter charged with their deep healths
43To their boon voyage, and to second that,
44Flamineo calls to have a valuating-horse
45Maintain their sport. The virtuous Marcello
46Is innocently plotted forth the room,
47Whilst your eye saw the rest, and can inform you
48The engine of all.

BRACHIANO

49It seems Marcello, and Flamineo
50Are both committed.

CONJUROR

Are both committed. Yes, you saw them guarded,
51And now they are come with purpose to apprehend
52Your mistress, fair Vittoria; we are now
53Beneath her roof: ‘twere fit we instantly
54Make your eye saw the rest, and can inform you
55The engine of all.
56Make out by some back postern.

BRACHIANO

Make out by some back postern. Noble friend,
57You bind me ever to you; this shall stand
58As the firm seal annexed to my hand
59It shall enforce a payment.

Exit BRACHIANO

CONJUROR

It shall enforce a payment. Sir I thank you.
60Both flowers and weeds spring when the sun is warm,
61As great men do great good, or else great harm.

Exit CONJUROR

[Act III, Scene i]

Enter FRANCISCO, and MONTICELSO, their CHANCELLOR and REGISTER

FRANCISCO

1You have dealt discreetly to obtain the presence
2Of all the grave lieger ambassadors
3To hear Vittoria’s trial.

MONTICELSO

To hear Vittoria’s trial. ‘Twas not ill,
4For sir you know we have nought but circumstances
5To charge her with, about her husband’s death;
6Their approbation therefore to the proofs
7Of her black lust, shall make her infamous
8To all our neighbouring kingdoms. I wonder
9If Brachiano will be here.

FRANCISCO

If Brachiano will be here. O fie,
10‘Twere impudence too palpable.

[Exeunt]

Enter FLAMINEO and MARCELLO guarded, and a LAWYER

LAWYER

11What, are you in by the week? So -I will not try now whether thy wit be close prisoner: methinks none should sit upon thy sister but old whore-masters, —

FLAMINEO

12Or cuckholds, for your cuckhold is your most terrible tickler of lechery: whore-masters would serve, for none are judges at tilting, but those that have been old tilters.

LAWYER

13My lord Duke and she have been very private.

FLAMINEO

14Your are a dull ass; ‘tis threat’ned they have been very Public.

LAWYER

15If it can be proved they have but kiss’d one another.

FLAMINEO

16What then?

LAWYER

17My lord cardinal will ferret them, —

FLAMINEO

18A cardinal I hope will not catch conies.

LAWYER

19For to sow kisses (mark what I say), to sow kisses, is to reap lechery, and I am sure a woman that will endure kissing is half won.

FLAMINEO

20True, her upper part by that rule; if you will win her nether

21part too, you know what follows.

LAWYER

22Hark, the ambassadors are lighted, —

FLAMINEO

23[aside] I do put on this feigned garb of mirthaparte
24To gull suspicion.

MARCELLO

To gull suspicion. O my unfortunate sister!
25I would my dagger’s point had cleft her hearth
26When she first saw Brachiano. You ‘tis said,
27Were made his engine, and his stalking-horse
28To undo my sister.

FLAMINEO

To undo my sister. I made a kind of path
29To her and mine own preferment.

MARCELLO

To her and mine own preferment. Your ruin.

FLAMINEO

30Hum! Thou art a soldier,
31Followest the great Duke, feedest his victories,
32As witches do their serviceable spirits,
33Even with thy prodigal blood; what hast got?
34But like the wealth of capitains, a poor handful,
35Which in thy palm thou bear’st, as men hold water;
36Seeking to gripe it fast, the frail reward
37Steals throught thy fingers.

MARCELLO

Steals throught thy fingers. Sir, —

FLAMINEO

Steals throught thy fingers. Sir, — Thou hast scarce maintenance
38To keep thee in fresh chamois.

MARCELLO

To keep thee in fresh chamois. Brother!

FLAMINEO

To keep thee in fresh chamois. Brother! Hear me, —
39And thus when we have even poured ourselves
40Into great fights, for their ambition
41Or idle spleen, how shall we find reward,
42But as we seldom find the mistletoe
43Sacred to physic on the builder oak
44Without a mandrake by it, so in our quest of gain.
45Alas the poorest of their forc’d dislikes
46At a limb proffers, but at hearth it strikes:
47This is lamented doctrine.

MARCELLO

This is lamented doctrine. Come, come.

FLAMINEO

48When age shall turn thee
49White as a blooming hawthorn, —

MARCELLO

White as a blooming hawthorn, — I’ll interrupt you.
50For love of virtue bear an honest hearth,
51And stride over every politic respect,
52Which where they most advance they most infect.
53Were I your father, as I am your brother,
54I should not be ambitious to leave you
55A better patrimony.

Enter Savoy [Ambassador]

FLAMINEO

A better patrimony. I’ll think on’t, —
56The lord ambassadors.

Here there is a passage of the lieger Ambassadors over the stage severally. Enter French Ambassador.

LAWYER

57O my sprightly Frenchman, do you know him? He’s an admirable tilter.

FLAMINEO

58I saw him at last tilting; he showed like a pewter candle-stick fashioned like a man in armour, holding a tilting staff in his hand, little bigger than a candle of twelve i’th’ pound.

LAWYER

59O but he’s an excellent horseman.

FLAMINEO

60A lame one in his lofty tricks; he sleeps o’ horseback like a poulter, —

Enter English and Spanish [Ambassadors]

LAWYER

61Lo you my Spaniard.

FLAMINEO

62Exeunt He carries his face in’s ruff, as I have seen a serving-man carry glasses in a cypress hat-band, monstrous steady for fear of breaking. He looks like the claw of a blackbird, first salted and then broiled in a candle.

[Act III, Scene ii]

THE ARRAINGMENT OF VITTORIA

Enter FRANCISCO, MONTICELSO, the six lieger Ambassadors, BRACHIANO, VITTORIA, [ZANCHE, FLAMINEO, MARCELLO,] LAWYER, and a guard

MONTICELSO

1Forbear my lord, here is no place assign’d you,
2The business by his holiness is left
3To our examination.

BRACHIANO

To our examination. May it thrive with you!

Lays a rich gown under him

FRANCISCO

4A chair there for his lordship.

BRACHIANO

5Forbear your kindness; and unbidden guest
6Should travel as Dutch women go to church;
7Bear their stools with them.

MONTICELSO

Bear their stools with them. At your pleasure sir.
8Stand to the table gentlewomen. Now signior
9Fall to your plea.

LAWYER

10Domine Judex converte oculos in hanc pestem mulierum

11corruptissimam.

VITTORIA

corruptissimam. What's he?

FRANCISCO

12A lowyer, that pleads against you.

VITTORIA

13Pray my lord, let him speak his usual tongue.
14I'll make no answer else.

FRANCISCO

I'll make no answer else. Why you understand Latin.

VITTORIA

15I do sir, but amongst this auditory
16Which come to hear my cause, the half or more
17May be ignorant in't.

MONTICELSO

May be ignorant in't. Go on sir.

VITTORIA

May be ignorant in't. Go on sir. By your favour,
18I will not have my accusation clouded
19In a strange tongue: all this assembly
20Shall hear what you can charge me with.

FRANCISCO

Shall hear what you can charge me with. Signior,
21You need not stand on't much; pray change your language.

MONTICELSO

22Oh for God sake: gentlewoman, your credit
23Shall be more famous by it.

LAWYER

Shall be more famous by it. Well then have at you.

VITTORIA

24I am at the mark sir, I'll gice aim to you,
25And tell you how near you shoot.

LAWYER

26Most literated judges, please your lordships,
27So to connive your judgements to the view
28Of this debauch'd and diversivolent woman
29Who such a black concatenation
30Of mischief hath effected, that to extirp
31The memory of't, must be the consummation
32Of her and her projections –

VITTORIA

Of her and her projections – What's all this? –

LAWYER

33Hold your peace.
34Exorbitant sins must have exulceration.

VITTORIA

35Surely my lords this lawyer here hath swallowed
36Some pothecary's bills, or proclamations.
37And now the hard and undigestible words
38Come up like stones we use give hawks for physic.
39Why this is Welsh to Latin.

LAWYER

Why this is Welsh to Latin. My lords, the woman
40Knows not her tropes nor figures, nor is perfect
41In the academy derivation
42Of grammatical elocution.

FRANCISCO

Of grammatical elocution. Sir your pains
43Shall be well spared, and your deep eloquence
44Be worthily applauded amongst those
45Which understand you.

LAWYER

Which understand you. My good lord.

FRANCISCO

Which understand you. My good lord. speaks this in a scorn Sir,
46Put up your papers in your fustian bag, –
47Cry mercy sir, 'tis buckram, -and acept
48My notion of your learn'd verbosity.

LAWYER

49I most graduatically thank your lordship.
50I shall have use for them elsewhere.

[Exit]

MONTICELSO

51I shall be plainer with you, and paint out
52Your follies in more natural red and white
53Than that upon your cheek.

VITTORIA

Than that upon your cheek. O you mistake.
54You raise a blood as noble in this cheek
55As ever was your mother's

MONTICELSO

56I must spare you till proof cry whore to that;
57Observe this creature here my honoured lords,
58A woman of a most prodigious spirit
59In her effected.

VITTORIA

In her effected. Honourable my lord,
60It doth not suit a reverend cardinal
61To play the lawyer thus –

MONTICELSO

62Oh your trade instructs your language!
63You see my lords what goodly fruit she seems,
64Yet like those apples travellers report
65To grow where Sodom and Gomorrah stood
66I will but touch her and you straight shall see
67She'll fall to soot and ashes.

VITTORIA

She'll fall to soot and ashes. Your envenom'd
68Pothecary should do't –

MONTICELSO

Pothecary should do't – I am resolved
69Were there a second paradise to lose
70This devil would betray it.

VITTORIA

This devil would betray it. O poor charity!
71Thou art seldom found in scarlet.

MONTICELSO

72Who knows not how, when several night by night
73Her gates were chok'd with coaches, and her rooms
74Outbrav'd the stars with several kind of lights
75When she did conterfeit a prince's court?
76In music, banquets and most riotous surfeits
77This whore, forsooth, was holy.

VITTORIA

This whore, forsooth, was holy. Ha? Whore? What's that?

MONTICELSO

78Shall I expound whore to you? Sure I shall:
79I'll give their perfect character. They are first
80Sweetmeats which rot the eater: in man's nostril
81Poison'd perfumes. They are coz'ning alchemy,
82Shipwracks in calmest weather! What are whores?
83Cold Russian winters, that appear so barren,
84They are the true material fire of hell,
85Worse than those tributes i'th' Low Countries paid,
86Exactions upon meat, drink, garments, sleep;
87Ay even on man's perdition, his sin.
88They are those brittle evidences of law
89Which forfeit all a wretched man's estate
90For leaving out one syllable. What are whores?
91They are those flattering bells have all one tune,
92At weddings, and at funerals: your rich whores
93Are only treasuries by extortion fill'd,
94And emptied by curs'd riot. They are worse,
95Worse than dead bodies, which are begg'd at gallows
96And wrought upon by surgeons, to teach man
97Wherein he is imperfect. What's a whore?
98She's like the guilty counterfeited coin
99Which whosoe'er first stamps it brings in trouble
100All that receive it –

VITTORIA

All that receive it – This character scapes me.

MONTICELSO

101You gentlewoman?
102Take from all beasts, and from all minerals
103They deadly poison.

VITTORIA

They deadly poison. Well what then?

MONTICELSO

They deadly poison. Well what then? I'll tell thee.
104I'll find in thee a pothecary's shop
105To sample them all.

FRENCH AMBASSADOR

To sample them all. She hath liv'd ill.

ENGLISH AMBASSADOR

106True, but the cardinal's too bitter.

MONTICELSO

107You know what whore is; next the devil, Adult'ry,
108Enters the devil, Murder.

FRANCISCO

Enters the devil, Murder. Your unhappy
109Husband is dead.

VITTORIA

Husband is dead. O he's a happy husband
110Now he owes nature nothing.

FRANCISCO

111And by a vaulting engine.

MONTICELSO

And by a vaulting engine. An active plot.
112He jump'd into his grave.

FRANCISCO

He jump'd into his grave. What a prodigy was't,
113That form some two yards' height a slender man
114Should break his neck?

MONTICELSO

Should break his neck? I'th'rushes.

FRANCISCO

Should break his neck? I'th'rushes. And what's more,
115Upon the instant lose all use of speech,
116All vital motion, like a man had lain
117Wound up three days. Now mark each circumstance.

MONTICELSO

118And look upon this creature was his wife.
119She comes not like a widow: she comes arm'd
120With scorn and impudence. Is this a mourning habit?

VITTORIA

121Had I foreknown his death as you suggest,
122I would have bespoke my mourning.

MONTICELSO

I would have bespoke my mourning. O you are cunning.

VITTORIA

123You shame your wit and judgement
124To call it so. What, is my just defence
125By him that is my judge call'd impudence?
126Let me appeal then from this Christian court
127To the uncivil Tartar.

MONTICELSO

To the uncivil Tartar. See my lords,
128She scandals our proceedings.

VITTORIA

She scandals our proceedings. Humbly thus,
129Thus low, to the most worthy and respected
130Lieger ambassadors, my modesty
131And womanhood I tender; but withal
132So entangled in a cursed accusation
133That my defence of force like Perseus,
134Must personate masculine virtue to the point.
135Find me but guilty, sever head from body:
136We'll part good friends: I scorn to hold my life
137At yours or any man's entreaty, sir.

ENGLISH AMBASSADOR

138She hath a brave spirit –

MONTICELSO

She hath a brave spirit – Well, well, such counterfeit jewels
139Make true ones oft suspected.

VITTORIA

Make true ones oft suspected. You are deceived.
140For know that all your strict-combined heads,
141Which strike against this mine of diamonds,
142Shall prove but glassen hammers, they shall break;
143These are but feigned shadows of my evils.
144Terryfy babes, my lord, with painted devils,
145I am past such needless plasy; for your names
146Of whore and murd'ress, they proceed from you,
147As if a man should spit against the wind,
148The filth returns in's face.

MONTICELSO

149Pray you mistress satisfy me one question:
150Who lodg'd beneath your roof that fatal night
151Your husband brake his neck?

BRACHIANO

Your husband brake his neck? That question
152Enforcheth me break silence: I was there.

MONTICELSO

153Your business?

BRACHIANO

Your business? Why I came to confort her,
154And take some course for sett'ling her estate,
155Because I heard her husband was in debt
156To you my lord.

MONTICELSO

To you my lord. He was.

BRACHIANO

To you my lord. He was. And 'twas stragely fear'd
157That you would cozen her.

MONTICELSO

That you would cozen her. Who made you overseer?

BRACHIANO

158Why my charity, my charity, which should flow
159From every generous and noble spirit,
160To orphans and to widows.

MONTICELSO

To orphans and to widows. Your lust.

BRACHIANO

161Cowardly dogs bark loudest. Sirrah priest,
162I'll talk with you hereafter, –Do you hear?
163The sword you frame of such an excellent temper,
164I'll sheathe in your own bowels:
165There are a number of thy coat resemble
166Your common post-boys.

MONTICELSO

Your common post-boys. Ha?

BRACHIANO

Your common post-boys. Ha? Your mercenary post-boys;
167Your letters carry truth, but 'tis your guise
168To fill your mouths with gross and impudent lies.

[He makes for the door]

SERVANT

169My lord your gown.

BRACHIANO

My lord your gown. Thou liest, 'twas my stool.
170Bestow't upon thy master that will challenge
171The rest o'th' household stuff; for Brachiano
172Was ne'er so beggarly, to take a stool
173Valence for his bed on't, or a demi-foot-cloth,
174For his most reverent moil; Monticelso,
175Exit BRACHIANO Nemo me impune lacessit.

MONTICELSO

176Your champion's gone.

VITTORIA

Your champion's gone. The wolf may prey the better.

FRANCISCO

177My lord there's great suspicion of the murder,
178But no sound proof who did it: for my part
179I do not think she hath a soul so black
180To act a deed so bloody; if she have,
181As in cold countries husbandmen plant vines,
182And with warm blood manure them, even so
183One summer she will bear unsavoury fruit,
184And ere next spring wither both branch and root.
185The act of blood let pass, only descend
186To matter of incontinence.

VITTORIA

To matter of incontinence. I discern poison
187Under your gilded pills.

MONTICELSO

188Now the Duke's gone, I will produce a letter,
189Wherein 'twas plotted he and you should meet,
190At an apothecary's summer-house,
191Down by the river Tiber: - view't my lords: –
192Where after wanton bathing and the heat
193Of a lascivious banquet. – I pray read it,
194I shame to speak the rest.

VITTORIA

I shame to speak the rest. Grant I was tempted
195Temptation to lust proves not the act,
196Casta est quam nemo rogavit,
197You read his hot love to me, buy you want
198My frosty answer.

MONTICELSO

My frosty answer. Frost i'th' dog-days! strange!

VITTORIA

199Condemn you me for that the Duke did love me?
200So may you blame some fair and crystal river
201For that some melancholic distracted man,
202Hath drown'd himself in't.

MONTICELSO

Hath drown'd himself in't. Truly drown'd indeed.

VITTORIA

203Sum up my faults I pray, and you shall find,
204That beauty and gay clothes, a merry heart,
205And a good stomach to a feast, are all,
206All the poor crimes that you can charge me with:
207In faitg my lord you might go pistol flies,
208The sport would be more noble.

MONTICELSO

The sport would be more noble. Very good.

VITTORIA

209But take you your course, it seems you have beggar'd me first
210And now would fain undo me; I have houses,
211Jewels, and a poor remnant of crusadoes,
212Would those would make you charitable.

MONTICELSO

Would those would make you charitable. If the devil
213Did ever take good shape behold his picture.

VITTORIA

214You have one virtue left,
215You will not flatter me.

FRANCISCO

You will not flatter me. Who brought this letter?

VITTORIA

216I am not compell'd to tell you.

MONTICELSO

217My lord Duke sent to you a thousand ducats,
218The twelfth of August.

VITTORIA

The twelfth of August. 'Twas to keep your cousin
219From prison; I paid use for't.

MONTICELSO

From prison; I paid use for't. I rather think
220'Twas interest for his lust.

VITTORIA

221Who says so but yourself? If you be my accuser
222Pray cease to be my judge, come from the bench,
223Give in your evidence 'gainst me, and let these
224Be moderators. My lord cardinal,
225Were your intelligencing ears as long
226As to my thoughts, had you an honest tongue
227I would not care though you proclaim'd them all.

MONTICELSO

228Go to, go to.
229After your goodly and vain-glorious banquet,
230I'll give you a choke-pear.

VITTORIA

I'll give you a choke-pear. O' your own grafting?

MONTICELSO

231You were born in Venice, honourably descended
232From the Vitelli; 'twas my cousin's fate, –
233Ill may I name the hour - to marry you;
234He bought you of your father.

VITTORIA

He bought you of your father. Ha?

MONTICELSO

He bought you of your father. Ha? He spent there in six months
235Twelve thousand ducats, and to my acquaintance
236Receiv'd in dowry with you not one julio:
237'Twas a hard penny-worth, the ware being so light.
238I yet but draw the curtain, now to your picture:
239You came from thence a most notorious strumpet,
240And so you have continued.

VITTORIA

And so you have continued. My lord.

MONTICELSO

And so you have continued. My lord. Nay hear me,
241You shall have time to prate. My lord Brachiano, –
242Alas I make but repetition,
243Of what is ordinary and Rialto talk,
244And ballated, and would be play'd o'th' stage,
245But that vice many times finds such loud friends
246That preachers are charm'd silent.
247You gentlemen Flamineo and Marcello,
248The court hath nothing now to charge you with,
249Only you must remain upon your sureties
250For your appearance.

FRANCISCO

For your appearance. I stand for Marcello.

FLAMINEO

251And my lord Duke for me.

MONTICELSO

252For you Vittoria, your public fault,
253Join'd to th' condition of the present time,
254Takes from you all the fruits of noble pity.
255Such a corrupted trial have you made
256Both of your life and beauty, and been styl'd
257No less in ominous fate than blazing stars
258To princes; here's your sentence: you are confin'd
259Unto a house of convertites and your bawd –

FLAMINEO

260[aside] Who I?aparte

MONTICESO

[aside] Who I? The Moor

FLAMINEO

[aside] Who I? The Moor [aside] O I am a sound man again.aparte

VITTORIA

261A house of convertites, what's that?

MONTICELSO

A house of convertites, what's that? A house
262Of penitent whores.

VITTORIA

Of penitent whores. Do the noblemen in Rome
263Erect ir for their wives, that I am sent
264To lodge there?

FRANCISCO

265You must have patience.

VITTORIA

You must have patience. I must first have vengance.
266I fain would know if you have your salvation
267By patent, that you proceed thus.

MONTICELSO

By patent, that you proceed thus. Away with her.
268Taje her hence.

VITTORIA

269A rape, a rape!

MONTICELSO

A rape, a rape! How?

VITTORIA

A rape, a rape! How? Yes, you have ravish'd justice,
270Forc'd her to do your pleasure.

MONTICELSO

Forc'd her to do your pleasure. Fie, she's mad –

VITTORIA

271Die with those pills in your most cursed maw,
272Should bring you health, or while you sit o'th' bench,
273Let your own spittle choke you.

MONTICELSO

Let your own spittle choke you. She's turn'd fury.

VITTORIA

274That the last day of judgement may so find you,
275And leave you the same devil you were before.
276Instruct me some good horse-leech to speak treason,
277For since you cannot take my life for deeds,
278Take it for words. O woman's poor revenge
279Which dwells but in the tongue! I will not weep,
280No I do scorn to call up one poor tear
281To fawn on your injustice; bear me hence,
282Unto this house of – what's your mitigating title?

MONTICELSO

283Of convertites.

VITTORIA

284It shall not be a house of convertities.
285My mind shall male it honester to me
286Than the Pope's palace, and more peaceable
287That thy soul, thought thou art a cardinal,
288Know this, and let it somewhat raise their richest light.

Exit VITTORIA [with ZANCHE, guarded]

Enter BRACHIANO

BRACHIANO

289Now you and I are friends sir, we'll shake hands,
290In a friend's grave, together: a fir place,
291Being the emblem of soft peace t'atone our hatred.

FRANCISCO

292Sir, what's the matter?

BRACHIANO

293I will not chase more blood from that lov'd cheek,
294You have lost too much already; fare you well.

[Exit]

FRANCISCO

295How strange these words sound? What's the interpretation?

FLAMINEO

296[aside] Good, this is a preface to the discovery of the Duchess' death. He carries ir well. Because now I cannot counterfeit a whining passion for the death of my lady, I will feign a mad humour for the disgrace of my sister, and that will keep off idle questions. Treason's tongue hath a villainous palsy in't; I will talk to any man, hear no man, and for a time appear a politic madam.

[Exit]

Enter GIOVANNI, Count LODOVICO

FRANCISCO

297How now my noble cousin; what, in black?

GIOVANNI

298Yes uncle, I was taught to imitate you
299In virtue, and you must imitate me
300In colours for your garments; my sweet mother
301Is, –

FRANCISCO

Is, – How? Where?

GIOVANNI

302Is there, no yonder; indeed sir I'll not tell you,
303For I shall make you weep.

FRANCISCO

304Is dead.

GIOVANNI

Is dead. Do not blame me now,
305I did not tell you so.

LODOVICO

I did not tell you so. She's dead my lord.

FRANCISCO

306Dead?

MONTICELSO

Dead? Blessed lady; thou art now above thy woes.
307Wilt please your lordships yo withdraw a little?

[Exeunt AMBASSADORS]

GIOVANNI

308What do the dead do, uncle? Do they eat,
309Hear music, go a-hunting, and be merry,
310As we that live?

FRANCISCO

311No coz; they sleep.

GIOVANNI

No coz; they sleep. Lord, Lord, that I were dead, –
312I have not slept these six nights. When do they wake?

FRANCISCO

313When God shall please.

GIOVANNI

When God shall please. Good God let her sleep ever.
314For I have known her wake an hundred nights,
315Was brine-wet with her tears. I am to complain to you sir.
316I'll tell you how they have used her now she's dead:
317They wrapp'd her in a cruel fold of lead,
318And would not let me kiss her.

FRANCISCO

And would not let me kiss her. Thou didst love her.

GIOVANNI

319I have often heard her say she gave me suck,
320And it should seem by that she dearly lov'd me,
321Since princes seldom do ir.

FRANCISCO

322O, all of my poor sister that remains!
323Take him away for God's sake.

[Exit GIOVANNI, attended]

MONTICELSO

Take him away for God's sake. How now my lord?

FRANCISCO

324Believe me I am nothing but her grave,
325And I shall keep her blessed memory
326Longer than thousand epitaphs.

[Exeunt]

[Act III, Scene iii]

Enter FLAMINEO as distracted [, MARCELLO and LODOVICO]

FLAMINEO

1We endure the strokes like anvils or hard steel,
2Till pain itself make us no pain to feel.
3Who shall do me right now? Is this the end of servide?
4I'd rather go weed garlic; travel through France, and
5be mine own ostler; wear sheep-skin linings; or shoes that
6stink of blancking; be ent'red into the list of the forty
7thousand pedlars in Poland.

Enter Savoy [Ambassador]

8Would I had rotted in some surgeon's house at Venice,
9built upon the pox as well as on piles, ere I had serv'd
10Brachiano

SAVOY AMBASSADOR

Brachiano You must have confort.

FLAMINEO

11Your comfortable words are like honey. They relish well in your mouth that's whole; but in mine that's wounded they go down as if the sting of the bee were in them. Oh they have wrought their purpose cunningly, as if they would not seem to do it of malice. In this a politician imitates the devil, as the devil imitates a cannon. Wheresoever he comes to do mischief, he comes with his backside towards you.

Enter the French [Ambassador]

FRENCH AMBASSADOR

12The proofs are evident.

FLAMINEO

13Enter English Ambassador You are happy in England, my lord; here they sell justice with those weights they press men to death with. O horrible salary! Proof! 'twas corruption. O gold, what a god art thou! And O man, what a devil art thou to be tempted by that cursed mineral! Yon diversivolent lawyer; mark him; knaves turn informers, as maggots turn to flies; you may catch gudgeons with either. A cardinal; - I would he would hear me, - there's nothing so holy but money will corrupt and putrify it, like victual under the line.

ENGLISH AMBASSADOR

14Fie, fie, Flamineo.

FLAMINEO

15[Exeunt Ambassadors] Bells ne'er ring well, till they are at their full pitch, and I hope yon cardinal shall never have the grace to pray well, till he come to the scaffold. 16If they were rack'd now to know the conferacy! But your noblemen are privileged from the rack; and well may. For a little thing would pull some of them a' pieces afore they came yo their arraingment. Religion; o how it is commeddled with policy. The first bloodshed in the world happened about religion. Would I were a Jew.

MARCELLO

17O, there are too many.

FLAMINEO

18You are deceiv'd. There are not Jews enough; priests enough, nor gentlemen enough.

MARCELLO

19How?

FLAMINEO

20I'll prove it. For if there were Jews enough, so many Christians would not turn usurers; if priests enough, one many early mushrooms, whose best growth sprang from a dunghill, should not aspire to gentility. Farewell. Let others live by begging. Be thou one of them; practise the art of Wolner in England to swallow all's given thee; and let one purgation make thee as hungry again as fellows that work in a sawpit. I'll go hear the streech-owl.

Exit

LODOVICO

21[aside] How dares this banish'd count return to Rome,aparte
22His pardon not yet puuchas'd? I have heard
23The deceas'd Duchess gave him pension,
24And that he came along from Padua
25I'th' train of the young prince. There's somewhat in't.
26Physicians, that cure poisons, still do work
27With counterpoisons.

MARCELLO

With counterpoisons. Mark this strange encounter.

FLAMINEO

28The god of melancholy turn thy gall to poison,
29And let the stigmatic wrinkles in thy face,
30Like to the boisterous waves in a rough tide
31One still overtake another.

LODOVICO

One still overtake another. I do thank thee
32And I do wish ingeniously for thy sake
33The dog-days all year long.

FLAMINEO

The dog-days all year long. How croaks the raven?
34Is our good Duchess dead?

LODOVICO

Is our good Duchess dead? Dead.

FLAMINEO

Is our good Duchess dead? Dead. O fate!
35Misfortune comes like the crowner's bussines,
36Huddle upon huddle.

LODOVICO

37Shalt thou and I join housekeeping?

FLAMINEO

Shalt thou and I join housekeeping? Yes, content.
38Let's be unsociably sociable.

LODOVICO

39Sit some three days together, and discourse.

FLAMINEO

40Only with making faces;
41Lie in our clothes.

LODOVICO

42With faggots for our pillows.

FLAMINEO

With faggots for our pillows. And be lousy.

LODOVICO

43In taffeta linings; that's gentle melancholy;
44Sleep all day.

FLAMINEO

Sleep all day. Yes: and like your melancholic hare
45Feed after midnight.

Enter ANTONELLI [and GASPARO, laughing]

46We are observed: see how yon couple grieve.

LODOVICO

47What a strange creature is a laughing fool,
48As if a man were created to no use
49But only to show his teeth.

FLAMINEO

But only to show his teeth. I'll tell the what,
50It would do well instead of looking-glasses
51To set one's dace each morning by a saucer
52Of a witch's congealed bood.

LODOVICO

Of a witch's congealed bood. Precious girn, rogue.
53We'll never part.

FLAMINEO

We'll never part. Never: till the beggary of courtiers,
54The discontent of churchmen, want of soldiers,
55And all the creatures that hang manacled,
56Worse than strappado'd, on the lowest felly
57Of Fortune’s wheel be taught in our two lives
58To scorn that world wich life of means deprives.

ANTONELLI

59My lord I bring good news. The Pope on's death-bed,
60At th'earnest suit of the great Duke of Florence,
