61Hath sign'd your pardon, and restor'd unto you –

LODOVICO

62I thank you for your news. Look up again
63Flamineo, see my pardon.

FLAMINEO

Flamineo, see my pardon. Why do you laugh?
64There was no such condition in our covenant.

LODOVICO

There was no such condition in our covenant. Why?

FLAMINEO

65You shall not seem a happier man that I;
66You know our vow sir, if you will be merry,
67Do it i'th' like posture, as if some great man
68Sat while his enemy were executed:
69Though it be very lechery unto thee,
70Do't with a crabbed politician's face.

LODOVICO

71Your sister is a damnable whore.

FLAMINEO

Your sister is a damnable whore. Ha?

LODOVICO

72Look you; I spake that laughing.

FLAMINEO

73Dost ever think to speak again?

LODOVICO

Dost ever think to speak again? Do you hear?
74Wilt sell me forty ounces of her blood,
75To water a mandrake?

FLAMINEO

To water a mandrake? Poor lord, you did vow
76To live a lousy creature.

LODOVICO

To live a lousy creature. Yes; –

FLAMINEO

To live a lousy creature. Yes; – Like one
77That had for ever forfeited the daylight,
78By being in debt, –

LODOVICO

By being in debt, – Ha, ha!

FLAMINEO

79I do not greatly wonder you do break:
80Your lordship learn't long since. But I'll tell you, –

LODOVICO

81What?

FLAMINEO

What? And't shall stick by you.

LODOVICO

What? And't shall stick by you. I long for it.

FLAMINEO

82This laughter scurvily becomes your face;
83Strikes him If you will not be melancholy, be angry.
84See, now I laugh too.

MARCELLO

85You are to blame, I'll force you hence.

LODOVICO

You are to blame, I'll force you hence. Unhand me.

Exit MAR[CELLO] & FLAM[INEO]

86That e'er I should be forc'd to right myself,
87Upon a pander!

ANTONELLI

Upon a pander! My lord.

LODOVICO

88H'had been as good meet with his fist a thunderbolt.

GASPARO

89How this shows!

LODOVICO

How this shows! Ud's death, how did my sword miss him?
90These rogues that are most weary of their lives,
91Sill scape the greatest dangers.
92A pox upon him: all his reputation; –
93Nay all the goodness of his family; –
94Is not worth half this earthquake.
95I learnt it of no fencer to shake thus;
96Come, I'll forget him, and go drink some wine.

Exeunt

[Act IV, Scene I]

Enter FRANCISCO and MONTICELSO

MONTICELSO

1Come, come my lord, untie your folded thoughts,
2And let them dangle loose as a bride's hair.
3Your sister's poisoned.

FRANCISCO

Your sister's poisoned. Far be it from my thoughts
4To seek revenge.

MONTICELSO

To seek revenge. What, are you turn'd all marble?

FRANCISCO

5Shall I defy him, and impose a war
6Most burthensome on my poor subjects' necks,
7Which at my will I have not power to end?
8You know; for all the murders, rapes,, and thefts,
9Committed in the horrid lust of war,
10He that unjustly caus'd it first proceed,
11Shall find it in his grave and in his seed.

MONTICELSO

12That's not the course I'd wish you: pray, observe me.
13We see that undermining more prevails
14That doth the cannon. Bear you wrongs conceal'd,
15And, patient as the tortoise, let this camel
16Stalk o'er your back unbruis'd: sleep with the lion,
17And let this brood of secure foolish mice
18Play with your nostrils; till the time be ripe
19For th' bloody audit, and the fatal gripe:
20Aim like a cunning fowler, close one eye,
21That you the better may your game espy.

FRANCISCO

22Free me my innocence, from treacherous acts:
23I know there's thunder yonder: and I'll stand,
24Like a safe valley, which low bends the knee
25To some aspiring mountain: since I know
26Treason, like spiders weaving nets for flies,
27By her foul work is found, and in it dies.
28To pass away these thoughts, my honour'd lord,
29It is reported you possess a book
30Wherein you have quoted, by intelligence,
31The names of all notorious offenders
32Lurking about the city.

MONTICELSO

Lurking about the city. Sir I do;
33And some there are which call it my black book:
34Well may the title hold: for thought it teach not
35The art of conjuring, yet in it lurk
36The names of many devils.

FRANCISCO

The names of many devils. Pray let's see it.

MONTICELSO

37I'll fetch it to your lordship.

Exit MONTICELSO

FRANCISCO

I'll fetch it to your lordship. Monticelso,
38I will not trust thee, but in all my plots
39I'll rest as jealous as a town besieg'd.
40Thou canst not reach what I intend to act;
41Your flax soon kindles, soon is out again,
42But gold slow heats, and long will hot remain.

Enter MONT[ICELSO] presents FRAN[CISCO] with a book

MONTICELSO

43'Tis here my lord.

FRANCISCO

44First your intelligencers, pray let's see.

MONTICELSO

45Their number rises strangely,
46And some of them
47You'd take for honest men.
48Next are panders.
49These are your pirates: and these following leaves,
50For base rogues that undo young gentlemen
51By taking up commodities: for politic bankrupts:
52For fellows that are bawds to their own wives,
53Only to put off horses and slight jewels,
54Clocks, defac'd plate, and such commodities,
55At birth of their first children.

FRANCISCO

At birth of their first children. Are there such?

MONTICELSO

56These are for imprudent bawds,
57That go in men's apparel; for users
58That share with scriveners for their good reportage:
59For lawyers that will antedate their writs:
60And some divines you might find folded there,
61But that I slip them o'er for conscience' sake.
62Here is a general catalogue of knaves.
63A man might study all the prisons o'er,
64Yet never attain this knowledge.

FRANCISCO

Yet never attain this knowledge. Murderers.
65Fold down the leaf I pray.
66Good my lord let me borrow this strange doctrine.

MONTICELSO

67Pray us't my lord.

FRANCISCO

Pray us't my lord. I do assure your lordship,
68You are a worthy member of the state,
69And have done inginite good in your discovery
70Of these offenders.

MONTICELSO

Of these offenders. Somewhat sir.

FRANCISCO

Of these offenders. Somewhat sir. O God!
71Better than tribute of wolves paid in England,
72'Twill hang their skins o'th' hedge.

MONTICELSO

'Twill hang their skins o'th' hedge. I must make bold
73To leave your lordship.

FRANCISCO

To leave your lordship. Dearly sir, I thank you;
74If any ask for me at court, report
75You have left me in the company of knaves.

Exit MONT[ICELSO]

76I gather now by this, some cunning fellow
77That's my lord's officer, one that lately skipp'd
78From a clerk's desk up to a justice' chair,
79Hath made this knavish summons; and intends,
80As th'Irish rebels wont were to sell heads,
81So to make prize of these. And thus it happens,
82Your poor rogues pay for't, which have not the means
83To present bribe in fist: the rest o'th' band
84Are raz'd out of the knaves' record; or else
85My lord he winks at them with easy will,
86His man grows rich, the knaves are the knaves still.
87But to the use I'll make of it; it shall serve
88To point me out a list of murderers,
89Agents for any villainy. Did I want
90Ten leash of courtezans, it would furnish me;
91Nay laundress three armies. That in so little paper
92Should lie th'undoing of so many men!
93'Tis not so big as twenty declarations.
94See the corrupted use some make of books:
95Divinity, wrested by some factious blood,
96Draws swords, swells battles, and o'erthrows all good.
97To fashion my revenge more seriously,
98Let me remember my dead sister's face:
99Call for her picture: no; I'll close mine eyes,
100And in a melancholic thought I'll frame

Enter ISABEL[L]A'S Ghost

101Her figure 'fore me. Now I ha't - - - how strong
102Imagination works! How she can frame
103Things which are not! Methinks she stands afore me;
104And by the quick idea of my mind,
105Were my skill pregnant, I could draw her picture.
106Thought, as a subtle juggler, makes us deem
107Things supernatural, which have cause
108Common as sickness. 'Tis my melancholy.
109How cam'st thou by thy death? - - - How idle am I
110To question my own idleness - - - Did ever
111Man dream awake till now? - - - Remove this object,
112Out of my brain with't: what have I to do
113With tombs, or death-beds, funerals, or tears,
114That have to meditate upon revenge?

[Exit Ghost]

115So now 'tis ended, like an old wives' story.
116Statesmen think often they see stranger sights
117Than madmen. Come, to this weighty business.
118My tragedy must have some idle mirth in't,
119Else it will never pass. I am in love,
120In love with Corombona, and my suit
121He writes. Thus halts yo her in verse. –
122I have done it rarely: O the fate of princes!
123I am so us'd to frequent flattery,
124That being alone I now flatter myself;
125But it will serve; 'tis seal'd. [calls offstage] Bear this

Enter SERVANT

126To th'house of convertites; and watch your leisure
127To give it to the hands of Corombona,
128Or to the matron, when some followers
129Exit SERVANT Of Brachiano may be by. Away!
130He that deals all by strength, his wit is shallow:
131When a man's head goes through, each limb will follow.
132The engine for my business, bold Count Lodowick;
133'Tis gold must such an instrument procure,
134With empty fist no man doth falcons lure.
135Brachiano, I am now fit for thy encounter.
136Like the wild Irish I'll ne'er think thee dead,
137Till I can play at football with thy head.
138Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo.

Exit

[Act IV, Scene ii]

Enter the MATRON, and FLAMINEO

MATRON

1Should it be known the Duke hath such recourse
2To your imprison'd sister, I were like
3T'incur much damage by it.

FLAMINEO

T'incur much damage by it. Not a scruple.
4The pope lies on his death-bed, and their heads
5Are troubled now with other business
6Enter SERVANT Than guarding of a lady.

SERVANT

7[aside] Yonder's Flamineo in conferenceaparte
8With the Matrona.
9[To the MATRON] Let me speak with you.
10I would entreat you yo deliver for me
11This letter to the fair Vittoria.

MATRON

12I shall sir.

Enter BRACHIANO

SERVANT

I shall sir. With all care and secrecy;
13Hereafter you shall know me, and receive
14Thanks for this courtesy.

[Exit]

FLAMINEO

Thanks for this courtesy. How now? What's that?

MATRON

15A letter.

FLAMINEO

A letter. To my sister: I'll see't delivered.

[Exit MATRON]

BRACHIANO

16What's that you read Flamineo?

FLAMINEO

What's that you read Flamineo? Look.

BRACHIANO

17[reads] Ha? To the most unfortunate his best respected Vittoria –
18Who was the messenger?

FLAMINEO

Who was the messenger? I know not.

BRACHIANO

19I'll open't, were't her heart. What's here subscribed –
20Florence? This juggling is gross and palpable.
21I have found out the conveyance; read it, read it.

FLAMINEO

22(Reads the letter) Your tears I'll turn to triumphs, be but mine.
23Your prop is fall'n; I pity that a vine
24Which princes heretofore have long'd to gather,
25Wanting supporters, now should fade and wither.
26Wine i'faith, my lord, with lees would serve his turn.
27Your sad imprisonment I'll soon uncharm,
28And with a princely uncontrolled arm
29Lead you to Florence, where my love and care
30Shall hang your wishes in my silver hair.
31A halter on his strange equivocation.
32Nor for my years return me the sad willow:
33Who prefer blossoms before fruit that's mellow?
34Rotten on my knowledge with lying too long i'th' bed-straw.
35And all the lines of age this line convinces:
36The gods neves wax old, no more do princes.
37A pox on't, rear it, let's have no more atheists for God's sake.

BRACHIANO

38Ud's death, I'll cut her into atomies
39And let th'irregular north-wind sweep her up
40And blow her int' his nostrils. Where's this whore?

FLAMINEO

41That –? what do you call her?

BRACHIANO

That –? what do you call her? O, I could be mad,
42Prevent the curs'd disease she'll bring me to,
43And tear my hair off. Where's this changeable stuff?

FLAMINEO

44O'er head and ears in water, I assure you,
45She is not for your wearing.

BRACHIANO

She is not for your wearing. In your pander!

FLAMINEO

46What me, my lord, am I your dog?

BRACHIANO

47A blood-hound: do you brave? do you stand me?

FLAMINEO

48Stand you? Let those that have diseases run;
49I need no plasters.

BRACHIANO

I need no plasters. Would you be kick'd?

FLAMINEO

50Would you have your neck broke?
51I tell you Duke, I am not in Russia;
52My shins must be kept whole.

BRACHIANO

My shins must be kept whole. Do you know me?

FLAMINEO

53O my lord! Methodically.
54As in this world there are degrees of evils:
55So in this world there are degrees of devils.
56You're a great Duke; I your poor secretary.
57I look now for a Spanish fig, or an Italian sallet daily.

BRACHIANO

58Pander, ply your convoy, and leave your prating.

FLAMINEO

59All your kindness to me is like that miserable courtesy of Polyphemus to Ulysses; you reserve me to be devour'd last; you would dig turves out of my grave to feed your larks; that would be music to you. Come, I'll lead you to her.

BRACHIANO

60Do you face me?

FLAMINEO

61O sir I would not go before a politic enemy with my back towards him, though there were behind me a whirlpool.

Enter VITTORIA to BRACHIANO and FLAMINEO

BRACHIANO

62Can you read mistress? Look upon that letter;
63There are no characters nor hieroglyphics.
64You need no comment, I am grown your reciever;
65God's precious, you shall be a brave great lady,
66A stately and advanced whore.

VITTORIA

A stately and advanced whore. Say sir?

BRACHIANO

67Come, come, let's see your cabinet, discover
68Your treasury of love-letters. Death and furies,
69I'll see them all.

VITTORIA

I'll see them all. Sir, upon my soul,
70I have not any. Whence was this directed?

BRACHIANO

71Confusion on your politic ignorance!

[Gives her the letter]

72You are reclaimed, are you? I'll give you the bells
73And let you fly to the devil.

FLAMINEO

And let you fly to the devil. Ware hawk, my lord.

VITTORIA

74[reads] Florence! This is some treacherous plot, my lord.
75To me, he ne'er was lovely I protest,
76So much as in my sleep.

BRACHIANO

So much as in my sleep. Right: they are plots.
77Your beauty! O, ten thousand curses on't.
78How long have I beheld the devil in crystal?
79Thou hast led me, like an heathen sacrifice,
80With music, and with fatal yokes of flowers
81To my eternal ruin. Woman to man
82Is either a god or a wolf.

VITTORIA

Is either a god or a wolf. My lord.

BRACHIANO

Is either a god or a wolf. My lord. Away.
83We'll be as differing as two adamants;
84The one shall shun the other. What? Dost weep?
85Procure but ten of tht dissembling trade,
86Ye'ld furnish all the Irish funerals
87With howling, past wild Irish.

FLAMINEO

With howling, past wild Irish. Fie, my lord.

BRACHIANO

88That hand, that crused hand, which I have wearied
89With doting kisses! O my sweetest Duchess
90[to VITTORIA] Thy loose thoughts How lovely art thou now!
91Scatter like quicksilver; I was bewitch'd;
92For all the world speaks ill of thee.

VITTORIA

For all the world speaks ill of thee. No matter.
93I'll live so now I'll make that world recant
94And change her speeches. You did name your Duchess.

BRACHIANO

95Whose death God pardon.

VITTORIA

Whose death God pardon. Whose death God revenge
96On thee most godless Duke.

FLAMINEO

On thee most godless Duke. Now for two whirlwinds.

VITTORIA

97What have I gain'd by thee but infamy?
98Thou hast stain'd the spotless honour of my house,
99And frighted thence noble society:
100Like those, which sick o'th' palsy, and retain
101Ill-secnting foxes 'bout them, are still shunn'd
102By those of choicer nostrils. What do you call this house?
103Is this your palace? Did not the judge style it
104A house of penitent whores? Who sent me to it?
105Who hath the honour to advance Vittoria
106To this incontinent college? Is't not you?
107Is't not your high preferment? Go, go brag
108How many ladies you have undone, like me.
109Fare you well sir; let me hear no more of you.
110I had a limb corrupted to an ulcer,
111But I have cut it off: and now I'll go
112Weeping to heaven on crutches. For your gifts,
113I will return them all; and I do wish
114That I could make you full executor
115To all my sins. O that I could toss myself
116Into a grave as quickly: for all thou art worth
117I'll not shed one tear more; – I'll burst first.

She throws herself upon a bed

BRACHIANO

118I have drunk Lethe. Vittoria?
119My dearest happiness! Vittoria!
120What do you ail my love? Why do you weep?

VITTORIA

121Yes, I now weep poniards, do you see.

BRACHIANO

122Are not those matchless eyes mine?

VITTORIA

Are not those matchless eyes mine? I had rather
123They were not matches.

BRACHIANO

They were not matches. Is not this lip mine?

VITTORIA

124Yes: thus to bite it off, rather than give it thee.

FLAMINEO

125Turn to my lord, good sister.

VITTORIA

Turn to my lord, good sister. Hence you pander.

FLAMINEO

126Pander! Am I the author of your sin?

VITTORIA

127Yes. He's a base thief that a thief lets in.

FLAMINEO

128We're blown up, my lord, –

BRACHIANO

We're blown up, my lord, – Wilt thou hear me?
129Once to be jealous of thee is t'express
130That I will love thee everlastingly
131And never more be jealous.

VITTORIA

And never more be jealous. O thou fool,
132Whose greatness hath by much o'ergrown thy wit!
133What dar'st thou do, that I not dare to suffer,
134Excepting to be still thy whore? For that,
135In the sea's bottom sooner thou shalt make
136A bonfire.

FLAMINEO

A bonfire. O, no oaths for God's sake.

BRACHIANO

137Will you hear me?

VITTORIA

Will you hear me? Never.

FLAMINEO

138What a damn'd imposthume is a woman's will?
139[to BRACHIANO, aside] Fie, fie, my lord. Can nothing break it?
140Women are caught as you take tortoises,
141She must be turn'd on her back. -Sister, by this hand
142I am on your side.- Come, come, you have wrong'd her.
143What a strange credulous man were you, my lord,
144To think the Duke of Florence would love her?
145Will any mercer take another's ware
146When once 'tis tows'd and sullied? And, yet sister,
147How scurvily this frowardness becomes you!
148Young leverets stand not long; and women's anger
149Should, like their flight, procure a little sport;
150A full cry for a quarter of an hour;
151And then be put to th' dead quat.

BRACHIANO

And then be put to th' dead quat. Shall these eyes,
152Which have so long time dwelt upon your face,
153Be now put out?

FLAMINEO

Be now put out? No cruel landlady i'th' world,
154Which lends forth groats to broom-men, and takes use for them
155Would do't.
156Hand her, my lord, and kiss her: be not like
157A ferret to let go your hold with blowing.

BRACHIANO

158Let us renew right hands.

VITTORIA

Let us renew right hands. Hence.

BRACHIANO

159Never shall rage, or the forgetful wine,
160Make me commit like fault.

FLAMINEO

161Now you are i'th' way on't, follow't hard.

BRACHIANO

162Be thou at peace with me; let all the world
163Threaten the cannon.

FLAMINEO

Threaten the cannon. Mark his penitence.
164Best natures do commit the grossest fauls,
165When they're giv'n o'er to jealousy; as best wine
166Dying makes strongest vinegar. I'll tell you;
167The sea's more rough and raging than calm rivers,
168But nor so sweet nor wholesome. A quiet woman
169Is a still water under a great bridge.
170A man may shoot her safely.

VITTORIA

171O ye dissembling men!

FLAMINEO

O ye dissembling men! We suck'd that, sister,
172From women's breasts, in our first infancy.

VITTORIA

173To add misery to misery.

BRACHIANO

To add misery to misery. Sweetest.

VITTORIA

174Am I not low enough?
175Ay, ay, your good hearth gathers like a snowball
176Now your affection's cold.

FLAMINEO

Now your affection's cold. Ud's foot, it shall melt
177To a hearth again, or all the wine in Rome
178Shall run o'th' lees for't.

VITTORIA

179You hawk or dog should be rewarded better
180Than I have been. I'll speak not one word more.

FLAMINEO

181Stop her mouth,
182With a sweet kiss, my lord.
183So now the tide's turn'd the vessel's come about.
184He's a sweet armful. O we curl'd-hair'd men
185Are still most kind to women. This is well.

BRACHIANO

186That you should chide thus!

FLAMINEO

That you should chide thus! O, sir, your little chimneys
187Do ever cast most smoke. I sweat for you.
188Couple together with as deep a silence
189As did the Grecians in their wooden horse.
190My lord, supply your promises with deeds.
191You know that painted meat no hunger feeds.

BRACHIANO

192Stay-ingrateful Rome!

FLAMINEO

Stay-ingrateful Rome! Rome! It deserves
193To be call'd Barbary, for our villainous usage.

BRACHIANO

194Soft; the same project which the Duke of Florence,
195(Whether in love or gullery I know not)
196Laid down for her escape, will I pursue.

FLAMINEO

197And no time fitter than this night, my lord;
198The Pope being dead; and all the cardinals ent'red
199The convlave for th'electing a new Pope;
200The city in a great confusion;
201We may attire her in a page's suit,
202Lay her post-horse, take shipping, and amain
203For Padua.

BRACHIANO

204I'll instantly steal forth the Prince Giovanni,
205And make for Padua. You two with your old mother
206And young Marcello that attends on Florence,
207If you can work him to it, follow me.
208I will advance you all: for you Vittoria,
209Think of a duchess' title.

FLAMINEO

Think of a duchess' title. Lo you sister.

210Stay, my lord; I'll tell you a tale. The crocodile, which lives in the river Nilus, hath a worm breeds i'th' teeth of't, which puts it to extreme anguish: a little bird, no bigger than a wren, is barber-surgeon to this crocodile; flies into the jaws of't; picks out the worm; and brings present remedy. The fish, glad of ease but ingrateful to her that did it, that the bird may not talk largely of her abroad for non-payment, closeth her chaps intending to swallow her, ando so put her to perpetual silence. But nature loathing such ingratitude, hath arm'd this bird with a quill or prick on the head, top o'th' which wounds the crocodile i'th' mouth; forceth her open her bloody prision; and away flies the pretty tooth-picker from her cruel patient.

BRACHIANO

211Your application is, I have not rewarded
212The service you have done me.

FLAMINEO

The service you have done me. No my lord;

213You sister are the crocodile: you are blemish'd in your fame, my lord cures it. And thought the comparison hold not in every particle; yet observe, remember, what good the bird with the prick i'th' head hath done you; and scorn ingratitude.

214[aside] It may appear to some ridiculousaparte
215Thus to talk knave and madman; and sometimes
216Come in with a dried sentence, stuff'd with sage.
217But this allows my varying of shapes,
218Knaves do grow great by being great men's apes.

Exeunt

[Act IV, Scene iii]

Enter LODOVICO, GASPARO, and six Ambassadors. At another door [FRANCISCO] the Duke of Florence.

FRANCISCO

1So, my lord, I commented your diligence.
2Guard well the conclave, and, as the order ir,
3Let none have conference with the cardinals.

LODOVICO

4I shall, my lord. Room for the ambassadors!

GASPARO

5They're wondrous brave today: why do they wear
6These several habits?

LODOVICO

These several habits? O sir, they're knights
7Of several orders.
8That lord i'th' black cloak with the silver cross
9Is Knight of Rhodes; the next Knight of S. Michael;
10That of the Golden Fleece; the Frenchman there
11Knight of the Holy Ghost; my lord of Savoy
12Knight of th'Annunciation; the Englishman
13Is Knight of th'honoured Garter, dedicated
14Unto their saint, S. George. I could describe to you
15Their several institutions, with the laws
16Annexed to their orders; but that time
17Permits not such discovery.

FRANCISCO

Permits not such discovery. Where's Count Lodowick?

LODOVICO

18Here my lord.

FRANCISCO

Here my lord. 'Tis o'th' point of dinner time;
19Marshal the cardinals' service.

LODOVICO

Marshal the cardinals' service. Sir, I shall.

Enter SERVANTS with several dishes covered

20Stand, let me search your dish; who's this for?

SERVANT

21For my lord Cardinal Monticelso.

LODOVICO

22Who's this?

SERVANT

Who's this? For my Lord Cardinal of Bourbon.

FRENCH AMBASSADOR

23Why doth he search the dishes? To observe
24What meat is dress'd?

ENGLISH AMBASSADOR

What meat is dress'd? No sir, but to prevent
25Lest any letters should be convey'd in
26To brive or to solicit the advancement
27Of any cardinal. When first they enter
28'Tis lawful for the ambassadors of princes
29To enter with them, and to make their suit
30For any man their prince affecteth best;
31But after, till a general election,
32No man may speak with them.

LODOVICO

33You that attend on the lord cardinals
34Open the window, and receive their viands.

A CARDINAL

35You must return the servide; the lord cardinals
36Are busied 'bout electing of the Pope;
37They have given o'er scrutiny, and are fallen
38To admiration.

LODOVICO

To admiration. Away, away.

[Exeunt SERVANTS with dishes]

FRANCISCO

39I'll lay a thousand ducats you hear news
40Of a Pope presently. Hark; sure he's elected, –
41[The] Cardinal [of ARRAGON appears] on the terrace
42Behold! my lord of Arragon appears
43On the church battlements.

ARRAGON

44Denuntio vobis gaudiu, magnum. Reverendissimus Cardinals LORENZO de MONTICELSO electus est in sedem apostolicam, et eligit nomen PAULUM quartum.

OMNES

45Vivat Sanctus Pater Paulus Quartus.

[Enter SERVANT]

SERVANT

46Vittoria my lord –

FRANCISCO

Vittoria my lord – Well: what of her?

SERVANT

47Is fled the city –

FRANCISCO

Is fled the city – Ha?

SERVANT

Is fled the city – Ha? With Duke Brachiano.

FRANCISCO

48Fled? Where's the Prince Giovanni?

SERVANT

Fled? Where's the Prince Giovanni? Gone with his father.

FRANCISCO

49Let the Matrona of the convertites
50Be apprehended. Fled? O damnable!

[Exit SERVANT]

51[aside] How fortunate are my wishes. Why? 'Twas thisaparte
52I only labour'd. I did send the letter
53T'instruct him what to do. Thy fame, fond Duke,
54I first have poison'd; directed thee the way
55To marry a whore; what can be worse? This follows:
56The hand must act to drown the passionate tongue,
57I scorn to wear a sword and prate of wrong.

Enter MONTICELSO in state

MONTICELSO

58Concedimus vobis apostolicam benedictionem et remissionem peccatorum.

[FRANCISCO whispers to him]

59My lord reports Vittoria Corombona
60Is stol'n from forth the house of convertites
61By Brachiano, and they're fled the city.
62Now, though this be the first day of our seat,
63We cannot better please the divine power,
64That to sequester from the holy church
65These cursed persons. Make it therefore known,
66We do denounce excommunication
67Against them both: all that are theirs in Rome
68We likewise banish. Set on.

Exeunt [all except FRANCISCO and LODOVICO]

FRANCISCO

69Come dear Lodovico
70You have tane the sacrament to prosecute
71Th'intended murder.

LODOVICO

Th'intended murder. With all constancy.
72But, sir, I wonder you'll engage yourself
73In person, being a great prince.

FRANCISCO

In person, being a great prince. Divert me not.
74Most of this court are of my faction,
75And some are of my counsel. Noble friend,
76Our danger shall be 'like in this design;
77Give leave, part of the glory may be mine.

Enter MONTICELSO

MONTICELSO

78Why did the Duke of Florence with such care
79Labour your pardon? Say.

LODOVICO

80Italian beggars will resolve you that
81Who, begging of an alms, bid those they beg of
82Do good for their own sakes; or't may be
83He spreads his bounty with a sowing hand,
84Like kings, who many times give out of measure;
85Not for desert so much as for their pleasure.

MONTICELSO

86I know you're cunning. Come, what devil was that
87That you were raising?

LODOVICO

That you were raising? Devil, my lord?

MONTICELSO

That you were raising? Devil, my lord? I ask you
88How doth such compliment unto his knee,
89When he departed from you?

LODOVICO

When he departed from you? Why, my lord,
90He told me of a resty Barbary horse
91Which he would fain have brought to the career,
92The 'sault, and the ring-galliard. Now, my lord,
93I have a rare French rider.

MONTICELSO

I have a rare French rider. Take you heed:
94Lest the jade break your neck. Do you put me off
95With your wild horse-tricks? Sirrah you do lie.
96O, thou'rt a foul black cloud, and thou dost threat
97A violent storm.

LODOVICO

A violent storm. Storms are i'th' air, my lord;
98I am yoo low to storm.

MONTICELSO

I am yoo low to storm. Wretched creature!
99I know that thou art fashion'd for all ill,
100Like dogs, that once get blood, they'll ever kill.
101About some murder? Was't not?

LODOVICO

About some murder? Was't not? I'll not tell you;
102And yet I care not greatly if I do;
103Marry with this preparation. Holy Father,
104I come not yo you as an intelligencer,
105But as a penitent sinner. What I utter
106Is in confession merely; which you know
107Must never be reveal'd.

MONTICELSO

Must never be reveal'd. You have o'ertane me.

LODOVICO

108Sir I did love Brachiano's Duchess dearly;
109Or rather I pursued her with hot lust,
110Though she ne'er knew on't. She was poison'd;
111Upon my soul she was: for which I have sworn
112T'avenge her murder.

MONTICELSO

T'avenge her murder. To the Duke of Florence?

LODOVICO

113To him I have.

MONTICELSO

To him I have. Miserable creature!
114If thou persist in this, 'tis damnable.
115Dost thou imagine thou canst slide on blood
116And not be tained with a shameful fall?
117Or, like the black and melancholic yew-tree,
118Dost think to root thyself in dead men's graves,
119And yet to prosper? Instruction to thee
120Comes like sweet showers to over-hard'ned ground:
121They wet, but pierce not deep. And so I leave thee
122With all the Furies hanging 'bout thy neck,
123Till by thy penitence thou remove this evil,
124In conjuring from thy breast that cruel devil.

Exit MON[TICELSO]

LODOVICO

125I'll give it o'er. He says 'tis damnable:
126Besides I did expect his suffrage,
127By reason of Camillo's death.

Enter SERVANT and FRANCISCO

FRANCISCO

128Do you know that count?

SERVANT

Do you know that count? Yes, my lord.

FRANCISCO

129Bear him these thousand ducats to his lodging;
130Tell him the Pope hath sent them. Happily
131[Exit] That will confirm more than all the rest.

SERVANT

[Exit] That will confirm more than all the rest. Sir.

[SERVANT delievers purse of money to LODOVICO]

LODOVICO

132To me sir?

SERVANT

133His Holiness hath sent you a thousand crowns,
134And wills you, if you travel, to make him
135Your patron for intelligence.

LUDOVICO

Your patron for intelligence. His creature
136[Exit SERVANT] Ever to be commanded.
137Why now 'tis come about. He rail'd upon me;
138And yet these crowns were told out and laid ready,
139Before he knew my voyage. O the art,
140The modest form of greatness! that do sit
141Like brides at wedding dinners, with their looks turn'd
142From the least wanton jests, their puling stomach
143Sick of the modesty, when their thoughts are loose,
144Even acting of those hot and lustful sports
145Are to ensue about midnight: such his cunning!
146He sounds my depth thus with a golden plummet;
147I am doubty arm'd now. Now to th'act of blood;
148There's but three Furies found in spacious hell;
149But in a great man's breast three thousand dwell.

[Exit]

[Act V, Scene i]

A passage over the stage of BRACHIANO, FLAMINEO, MARCELLO, HORTENSIO, [VITTORIA] COROMBONA, CORNELIA, ZANCHE and others

[Enter FLAMINEO and HORTENSIO]

FLAMINEO

1In all the weary minutes of my life,
2Day ne'er broke up till now. This marriage
3Confirms me happy.

HORTENSIO

Confirms me happy. 'Tis a good assurance.
4Saw you not yet the Moor that's come to court?

FLAMINEO

5Yes, and conferr'd with him i'th' Duke's closet;
6I have not seen a goodlier personage,
7Nor ever talk'd with man better experienc'd
8In state affairs or rudiments of war.
9He hath by report serv'd the Venetian
10In Candy these twice seven years, and been chief
11In many a bold design.

HORTENSIO

In many a bold design. What are those two
12That bear him company?

FLAMINEO

13Two noblemen of Hungary, that living in the emperor's service as commanders, eight years since, contrary to the expectation of all the court ent'red into religion, into the strict order of Capuchins: but being not well settled in their undertaking they left their order and returned to court: for which being after troubled in conscience, they vowed their service agaist the enemies of Christ; went to Malta; were there knighted; and in their return back, at this great solemnity, they are resolved for ever to forsake the world, and settle themselves here in a house of Capuchins in Padua.

HORTENSIO

14'Tis strange.

FLAMINEO

15One thing makes it so. They have vowed for ever to wear next their bare bodies those coats of mail they served in.

HORTENSIO

16Hard penance. Is the Moor a Christian?

FLAMINEO

17He is.

HORTENSIO

18Why proffers he his service to our Duke?

FLAMINEO

19Because he understands there's like to grow
20Some wars between us and the Duke of Florence,
21In which he hopes employment.
22I never saw one in a stern bold look
23Wear more command, nor in a lofty phrase
24Express more knowing, or more deep contempt
25Of our slight airy courtiers. He talks
26As if he had travell'd all the princes' courts
27Of Christendom; in all things strives t'express
28That all that should dispute with him may know,
29Glories, like glow-worms, afar off shine bright
30But look'd to near, have neither heat nor light.
31The Duke!

Enter BRACHIANO, [FRANCISCO, Duke of] Florence disguised like Mulinassar; LODOVICO, ANTONELLI, GASPARO, FERNESE having their swords and helmets.

BRACHIANO

32You are nobly welcome. We have heard at full
33Your honourable service 'gainst the Turk.
34To you, brave Mulinassar, we assign
35A competent pension: and are inly sorrow,
36The vows of those two worthy gentlemen
37Make them incapable of our proffer'd bounty.
38Your wish is you may leave your warlike swords
39For monuments in our chapel. I accept it
40As a great honour done me, and must crave
41Your leave to furnish out our Duchess' revels.
42Only one thing, as the last vanity
43You e'er shall view, deny me not to stay
44To see a barriers prepar'd tonight;
45You shall have private standings. It hath pleas'd
46The great ambassadors of several princes
47In their return from Rome to their own countries
48To grace our marriage, and to honour me
49With such a kind of sport.

FRANCISCO

With such a kind of sport. I shall persuade them
50To stay, my lord.

BRACHIANO

To stay, my lord. Set on there to the presence.

Exeunt BRACHIANO, FLAMINEO and [HORTENSIO]

LODOVICO

51Noble my lord, most fortunately welcome,

The conspirators here embrace

52You have our vows seal'd with the sacrament
53To second your attempts.

GASPARO

To second your attempts. And all things ready.
54He could not have invented his own ruin,
55Had he despair'd, with more propriety.

LODOVICO

56You would not take my way.

FRANCISCO

You would not take my way. 'Tis better ordered.

LODOVICO

57T'have poison'd his prayer book, or a pair of beads,
58The pommel of his saddle, his looking-glass,
59Or th'handle of his racket. O that, that!
60That while he had been bandying at tennis,
61He might have sworn himself to hell, and struck
62His soul into the hazard! O my lord!
63I would have our plot be ingenious,
64And have it hereafter recorded for example
65Rather than borrow example.

FRANCISCO

Rather than borrow example. There's no way
66More speeding than this thought on.

LODOVICO

More speeding than this thought on. On then.

FRANCISCO

67And yet methinks that this revenge is poor,
68Because it steals upon him like a thief;
69To habe tane him by the cask in a pitch'd field,
70Led him to Florence!

LODOVICO

Led him to Florence! It had been rare. -And there
71Have crown'd him with a wreath of stinking garlic,
72T'have shown the sharpness of his government,
73And rankness of his lust. Flamineo comes.

Exeunt LODOVICO, ANTONELLI [and GASPARO]

Enter FLAMINEO, MARCELLO and ZANCHE

MARCELLO

74Why doth this devil haunt you? Say.

FLAMINEO

Why doth this devil haunt you? Say. I know not.
75For by this light I do not conjure for her.
76'Tis not so great a cunning as men think
77To raise the devil: for here's one up already;
78The greatest cunning were to lay him down.

MARCELLO

79She is your shame.

FLAMINEO

She is your shame. I prithee pardon her.
80In faith you see, women are like to burs;
81Where their affection throws them, there they'll stick.

ZANCHE

82That is my countryman, a goodly person;
83When he's at leisure I'll discourse with him
84In our own language.

FLAMINEO

In our own language. Exit ZANCHE I beseech you do.
85How is't brave soldier? O that I had seen
86Some of your iron days! I pray relate
87Some of your service to us.

FRANCISCO

88'Tis a ridiculous thing for a man to be his own chronicle; I did never wash my mouth with mine own praise for fear of getting a stinking breath.

MARCELLO

89You're too stoical. The Duke will expect other discourse from you.

FRANCISCO

90I shall never flatter him, I have studied man too much to do that. What difference is between the Duke and I? No more than between two bricks; all made of one clay. Only 't may be one in plac'd on the top of a turret; the other in the bottom of a well by mere chance; if I were plac'd as high as the Duke, I should stick as fast; make as fair a show; and bear out weater equally.

FLAMINEO

91If this soldier had a patent to beg in churches, then he would tell them stories.

MARCELLO

92I have been a soldier too.

FRANCISCO

93How have you thriv'd?

MARCELLO

94Faith, poorly.

FRANCISCO

95That's the mistery of peace. Only outsiders are then respected.As ships seem very great upon the river, which show very little upon the seas: so some men i'th' court seem Colossues in a chamber, who if they came into the fiel would appear pitiful pigmes.

FLAMINEO

96Give me a fair room yet hung with arras, and some great cardinal to lug me by th'ears as his endeared minion.

FRANCISCO

97And thou may'st do, -the devil knows what villainy.

FLAMINEO

98And safely.

FRANCISCO

99Right; you shall see in the country in harvest time, pigeons, thought they destroy never so much corn, the farmer dare not present the fowling-piece to them! Why? Because they belong to the lord of the manor; whilst your poor sparrows that belong to the Lord of heaven, they go to the pot for't.

FLAMINEO

100I will now give you some politic instruction. The Duke says he will give you pension; that's but bare promise: get it under his hand. For I have know men that have come for serving against the Turk; for three or four months they have had pension to boy them new wooden legs and fresh plasters; but after 'twas not to be had. And this miserable courtesy shows, as if a tormentor should give hot cordial drinks to one three-quarters dead o'th' rack, only to fetch the miserable soul again to endure more dog-days.

Enter HORTENSIO, a YOUNG LORD, ZANCHE and two more

101How now, gallants; what, are they ready for the barriers?

[Exit FRANCISCO]

YOUNG LORD

102Yes: the lords are putting on their armour.

HORTENSIO

103What's he?

FLAMINEO

104A new upstart: one that swears like a falc'ner, and will lie in the Duke's ear day by day like a maker of almanacs; and yet I knew him since he came to th'court smell worse of sweat than an under-tennis-court-keeper.

HORTENSIO

105Look you, yonder's your sweet mistress.

FLAMINEO

106Thou art my sworn brother; I'll tell thee, I do love that Moor, that witch, very constrainedly: she knows some of my villainy; I do love her, just as a man holds a wolf by the ears. But for fear of turning upon me, and pulling out my throat, I would let her go to the devil.

HORTENSIO

107I hear she claims marriage of thee.

FLAMINEO

108'Faith, I made to her some such dark promise, and in seeking to fly from't I run on, like a frighted dog with a bottle at's tail, that fain would bite it off and yet dares not look behind him. 109[to ZANCHE] Now my precious gipsy!

ZANCHE

110Ay, your love to me rather cools than heats.

FLAMINEO

111Marry, I am the sounder lover; we have many wenches about the town heat too fast.

HORTENSIO

112What do you think of these perfum'd gallants then?

FLAMINEO

113Their satin cannot save them. I am confident
114They have a certain spice of the disease.
115For they that sleep with dogs, shall rise with fleas.

ZANCHE

116Believe it! A little painting and gay clothes
117Make you loathe me.

FLAMINEO

118How? Love a lady for painting or gay apparel? I'll unkennel one example more of thee. Æsop had a foolish dog that let go the flesh to catch the shadow. I would have courtiers be better diners.

ZANCHE

119You remember your oaths.

FLAMINEO

120Lovers' oaths are like mariners' prayers, uttered in extremity; but when the tempest is o'er, and that the vessel leaves tumbling, they fall from protesting to drinking. And yet amongst gentlemen protesting and drinking go together, and agree as well as shoemakers and Westphalia bacon. They are both drawers on: for drink draws on protestation; and protestation draws on more drink. Is not this discourse better no than the morality of your sunburnt gentleman?

Enter CORNELIA

CORNELIA

121Is this your perch, you haggard? Fly to th'stews.

[Strikes ZANCHE]

FLAMINEO

122You should be clapp'd by th'heels now: strike i'th'court?

[Exit CORNELIA]

ZANCHE

123She's good for nothing but to make her maids
124Catch cold o'nights; they dare not usa a bedstaff,
125For fear f her light fingers.

MARCELLO

For fear f her light fingers. You're a strumpet.
126An impudent one.

FLAMINEO

An impudent one. Why do you kick her? Say,
127Do you think that she's like a walnut-tree?
128Must she be cudgell'd ere she bear good fruit?

MARCELLO

129She brags that you shall marry her.

FLAMINEO

She brags that you shall marry her. What then?

MARCELLO

130I had rather she were pitch'd upon a stake
131In some new-seeded garden, to affright
132Her fellow crows thence.

FLAMINEO

Her fellow crows thence. You're a boy, a fool,
133Be guardian to your hound, I am of age.

MARCELLO

134If I take her near you I'll cut her throat.

FLAMINEO

135With a fan of feathers?

MARCELLO

With a fan of feathers? And for you, I'll whip
136This folly from you.

FLAMINEO

This folly from you. Are you choleric?
137I'll purgue't with rhubarb.

HORTENSIO

I'll purgue't with rhubarb. O your brother!

FLAMINEO

I'll purgue't with rhubarb. O your brother! Hang him.
138He wrongs me most that ought t'offend me least.
139[to MARCELLO] I do suspect my mother play'd foul play
140When she conceiv'd thee.

MARCELLO

When she conceiv'd thee. Now by all my hopes,
141Like the two slaught'red sons of Œdipus,
142The very flames of our affection
143Shall turn two ways. Those words I'll make thee answer
144With thy heart blood.

FLAMINEO

With thy heart blood. Do; like the gesses in the progress,
145You know where you shall find me, –

MARCELLO

You know where you shall find me, – Very good.

[Exit FLAMINEO]

146And thou beest a noble friend, bear him my sword,
147And bid him fit the length on't.

YOUNG LORD

And bid him fit the length on't. Sir I shall

[Exeunt all but ZANCHE]

Enter FRANCISCO the Duke of Florence

ZANCHE

148[aside] He comes. Hence petty thought of my disgrace!aparte
149I ne'er lov'd my complexion till now,
150Cause I may boldly say without a blush,
151I love you.

FRANCISCO

I love you. Your love is untimely sown;
152There's a Spring at Michaelmas, but 'tis but a faint one.
153I am sunk in years, and I have vowed never yo marry.

ZANCHE

154Alas! poor maids get more lovers than husbands. Yet you may mistake my wealth. For, as when ambassadors are sent to congratulate princes, there's commonly sent along with them a rich present; so that though the prince like not the ambassador's person nor words, yet he likes well of the presentment. So I may come to you in the same manner, and be better loved for my dowry than my virtue.

FRANCISCO

155I'll think on the motion.

ZANCHE

156Do, I'll now detain you no longer. At your better leisure I'll tell you things shall startle your blood.

157Nor blame me that this passion I reveal;
158Lovers die inward that their flames conceal.

FRANCISCO

159[aside] Of all intelligente this may prove the best,aparte
160Sure I shall draw strange fowl from this foul nest.

Exeunt

[Act V, Scene ii]

Enter MARCELLO and CORNELIA [and a PAGE, who remains in the background]

CORNELIA

1I hear a whispering all about the court,
2You are to fight; who is your opposite?
3What is the quarrel?

MARCELLO

What is the quarrel? 'Tis an idle rumour.

CORNELIA

4Will you dissemble? Sure you do not well
5To fright me thus; you never look thus pale,
6But when you are most angry. I do charge you
7Upon my blessing; –nay I'll call the Duke,
8And he shall school you.

MARCELLO

And he shall school you. Publish not a fear
9Which would convert to laughter; 'tis not so.
10Was not this crucifix my father's?

CORNELIA

Was not this crucifix my father's? Yes.

MARCELLO

11I have heard you say, giving my brother suck,
12Enter FLAMINEO He took the crucifix between his hands,
13And broke a limb off.

CORNELIA

And broke a limb off. Yes: but 'tis mended.

FLAMINEO

14I have brought your weapon back.

FLAMINEO runs MARCELLO through

CORNELIA

I have brought your weapon back. Ha, O my horror!

MARCELLO

15You have brought it home indeed.

CORNELIA

You have brought it home indeed. Help! Oh he's murdered.

FLAMINEO

16Do you turn your gall up? I'll to sanctuary,
17And send a surgeon to you

[Exit]

Enter CARL[O,] HORT[ENSIO,] PEDRO

HORTENSIO

And send a surgeon to you How? O'th' ground?

MARCELLO

18O mother now remember what I told
19Of breaking off the crucifix: farewell.
20There are some sins which heaven doth duly punish
21In a whole family. This it is to rise
22By all dishonest means. Let all men know
23That tree shall long time keep a steady foot
24Whose branches spread no wider than the root.

CORNELIA

25O my perpetual sorrow!

HORTENSIO

O my perpetual sorrow! Virtuous Marcello.
26He's dead: pray leave him lady; come, you shall.

CORNELIA

27Alas he is not dead: he's in a trance. Why here's nobody shall get anything by his death. Let me call him again for God's sake.

LODOVICO

28I would you were deceiv'd.

CORNELIA

29O you abuse me, you abuse, me, you abuse me. How many have gone away this for lack of tendance; rear up's head, rear up's head. His bleeding inward will kill him.

HORTENSIO

30You see he is departed.

CORNELIA

31Let me come to him; give me him as he is; if he be turn'd to earth; let me but give him one hearty kiss, and you shall put us both into one coffin: fetch a looking-glass, see if his breath will not stain it; or pull out some feathers from my pillow, and lay them to his lips, -will you lose him for a little pains-taking?

HORTENSIO

32Your kindest office is to pray for him.

CORNELIA

33Alas! I would not pray for him yet. He may live lo lay me i'th' ground, and pray for me, if you'll let me come to him.

Enter BRACHIANO all armed, save the beaver, with FLAMINEO [and FRANCISCO]

BRACHIANO

34Was this your handiwork?

FLAMINEO

35It was my misfortunate.

CORNELIA

36He lies, he lies, he did not kill him: these have kill'd him, that would not let him be better look'd to.

BRACHIANO

37Have comfort my griev'd mother.

CORNELIA

38O you screech-owl.

HORTENSIO

39Forbear, good madam.

CORNELIA

40Let me go, let me go.

She runs to FLAMINEO with her knife drawn and coming to him lets it fall

41The God of heaven forgive thee. Dost not wonder
42I pray for thee? I'll tell thee what's the reason:
43I have scarce breath to number twenty minutes;
44I'd not spend that in cursing. Fare thee well –
45Half of thyself lies there: and may'st thou live
46To fill an hour-glass with his mould'res ashes,
47To tell how thou shouldst spend the time to come
48In blest repentance.

BRACHIANO

In blest repentance. Mother, pray tell me
49How came he by his death? What was the quarrel?

CORNELIA

50Indeed my younger boy presum'd too much
51Upon his manhood; gave him bitter words;
52Drew his sword first; and so I know not how,
53For I was out of my wits, he fell with's head
54Jus in my bosom.

PAGE

Jus in my bosom. This is not true madam.

CORNELIA

55I pray thee peace.
56One arrow's graz'd already; it were vain
57T'lose this: for that will nere be found again.

BRACHIANO

58Go, bear the body to Cornelia's lodging:
59And we command that none acquaint our Duchess
60With this sad accident: for you Flamineo,
61Hark you, I will not grant your pardon.

FLAMINEO

Hark you, I will not grant your pardon. No?

BRACHIANO

62Only a lease of your life. And that shall last
63But for one day. Thou shalt be forc'd each evening
64To renew it, or be hang'd.

FLAMINEO

To renew it, or be hang'd. At your pleasure.

LODOVICO sprinkles BRACHIANO'S beaver with a poison

65Your will is law now, I'll not meddle with it.

BRACHIANO

66You onve did brave me in your sister's lodging;
67I'll now keep you in awe for't. Where's our beaver?

FRANCISCO

68[aside] He calls for his destruction. Noble youth,aparte
69I pity thy sad fate. Now to the barriers.
70This shall his passage to the black lake further,
71The last good deed he did, he pardon'd murther.

Exeunt

[Act V, Scene iii]

Charges and shouts. They fight at barriers; first single pairs, then three to three.

Enter BRACHIANO and FLAMINEO with others [including GIOVANNI, VITTORIA, and FRANCISCO]

BRACHIANO

1An armourer! Ud's death, an armourer!

FLAMINEO

2Armourer; where's the armourer?

BRACHIANO

3Tear off my beaver.

FLAMINEO

Tear off my beaver. Are you hurt, my lord?

BRACHIANO

4Enter ARMOURER O my brain's on fire,
5The helmet is poison'd.

ARMOURER

The helmet is poison'd. My lord upon my soul –

BRACHIANO

6[Exit ARMOURER, guarded] Away with him to torture.
7There are some great ones that have hand in this,
8And near about me.

VITTORIA

And near about me. O my loved lord; poison'd?

FLAMINEO

9Remove the bar: here's unfortunate revels,
10Ent[er] 2 PHYSICIANS Call the physicians; a plague upon you;
11We have too much of your cunning here already.
12I fear the ambassadors are likewise poisoned.

BRACHIANO

13Oh I am gone already: the infection
14Fllies to the brain and hearth. O thou strong heart!
15There's such a covenant 'tween the world and it,
16They're loth to break.

GIOVANNI

They're loth to break. O my most loved father!

BRACHIANO

17Remove the boy away.
18Where's this good woman? Had I infinite worlds
19They were too little for thee. Must I leave thee?
20What say yon screech-owls, is the venom mortal?

PHYSICIANS

21Most deadly.

BRACHIANO

Most deadly. Most corrupted politic hangman!
22You kill without book; but your art to save
23Fails you as a oft as great men's needy friends.
24I that have given life to offending slaves
25And wretched murderers, have I not power
26To lengthen mine own a twelvemonth?
27[to VITTORIA] Do not kiss me, for I shall poison thee.
28This unction is sent from the great Duke of Florence.

FRANCISCO

29Sir be of confort.

BRACHIANO

30O thou soft natural death, that art joint-twin
31To sweetest slumber: no rought-bearded comet
32Stares on thy mild departure; the dull owl
33Beats not against thy casement: the hoarse wolf
34Scents not thy carrion. Pity winds thy corse,
35Whilist horror waits on pinces.

VITTORIA

Whilist horror waits on pinces. I am lost for ever.

BRACHIANO

36How miserable a thing it is to die
37'Mongst women howling!

[Enter LODOVICO and GASPARO disguised as Capuchins]

'Mongst women howling! What are those?

FLAMINEO

'Mongst women howling! What are those? Franciscans.
38They have brought the extreme unction.

BRACHIANO

39On pain of death, let no man name death to me,
40It is a word infinitely terrible.
41Withdraw into our cabinet.

Exeunt omnes praeter FRANCISCO and FLAMINEO

FLAMINEO

42To see what solitariness is about dying princes. As heterofore they have unpeopled towns; divorc'd friends, and made great houses unhospitable: so now, O justice! Where are their flatterers now? Flatterers are but the shadows of princes' bodies, the least thrick could makes them invisible.

FRANCISCO

43There's great moan made for him.

FLAMINEO

44'Faith, for some few hours salt water will run most plentifully in every office o'th'court. But believe it; most of them do but weep over their stepmothers' graves.

FRANCISCO

45How mean you?

FLAMINEO

46Why? They dissemble, as some men do that live within compass o'th' verge.

FRANCISCO

47Come you have thriv'd well under him.

FLAMINEO

48'Faith, like a wolf in a woman's breast; I have been fed with poultry: but money, understand me, I had as good a will to cozen him, as e'er an officer of them all. But I had not cunning enough to do it.

FRANCISCO

49What did'st thou think of him? 'Faith speak freely.

FLAMINEO

50He was a kind of statesman, that would sooner have reckon'd how many cannon-bullets he had discharged against a town, to count his expense that way, than how many of this valiant and deserving subjects he lost before it.

FRANCISCO

51O speak well of the Duke.

FLAMINEO

52I have done. Wilt hear some of my court wisdom? 53Enter LODOVICO To reprehend princes is dangerous: and to over-commend dome of them is palpable lying.

FRANCISCO

54How is it with the Duke?

LODOVICO

How is it with the Duke? Most deadly ill.
55He's fall'n into a strange distraction.
56He talks of battles and monopolies,
57Levying of taxes, and from that descends
58To the most brain-sick language. His mind fastens
59On twenty several objects, which confound
60Deep sense with folly. Such a fearful end
61May teach some men that bear too lofty crest,
62Though they live happiest, yet they die not best.
63He hath conferr'd the whole state of the dukedom
64Upon your sister, till the Prince arrive
65At mature age.

FLAMINEO

At mature age. There's some good luck in that yet.

FRANCISCO

66See here he comes.

Enter BRACHIANO, presented in a bed, VITTORIA and others [including GASPARO].

VITTORIA

67O my good lord!

These speeches are several kinds of distractions and in the action should appear so

BRACHIANO

O my good lord! Away, you have abus'd me.
68You have convey'd coin forth our territories;
69Bought and sold offices; oppress'd the poor,
70And I ne'er dreamt on't. Make up your accounts;
71I'll now be mine own steward.

FLAMINEO

I'll now be mine own steward. Sir, have patience.
72Indeed I am too blame.
73For did you ever hear the dusky raven
74Chide blackness? or was't ever know the devil
75Rail'd against cloven creatures?

VITTORIA

Rail'd against cloven creatures? O my lord!

BRACHIANO

76Let me have some quails to supper.

FLAMINEO

Let me have some quails to supper. Sir, you shall.

BRACHIANO

77No: some fried dog-fish. Your quails feed on poison; –
78That old dog-fox, that poitician Florence, –
79I'll forswear hunting and turn dog-killer;
80Rare! I'll be friends with him: for mark you, sir, one dog
81Still sets another a-barking: peace, peace,
82Yonder's a fine slave come in now.

FLAMINEO

Yonder's a fine slave come in now. Where?

BRACHIANO

83Why there.
84In a blue bonnet, and a pair of breeches
85With a great codpiece. Ha, ha, ha,
86Look you his codpiece is stuck full of pins
87With pearls o'th' head of them. Do not you know him?

FLAMINEO

88No my lord.

BRACHIANO

No my lord. Why 'tis the devil.
89I know him by a great rose he wears on's shoe
90To hide his cloven foot. I'll dispute with him.
91He's a rare linguist.

VITTORIA

He's a rare linguist. My lord here's nothing.

BRACHIANO

92Nothing? rare! nothing! When I want money
93Our treasury is empty; there is nothing.
94I'll not be used thus.

VITTORIA

I'll not be used thus. O! lie still my lord –

BRACHIANO

95See, see, Flamineo that kill'd his brother
96Is dancing on the ropes there: and he carries
97A money-bag in each hand, to keep him even,
98For fear of breaking's neck. And there's a lawyer
99In a gown whipt with velvet, stares and gapes
100When the money will fall. How the rogue cuts capers!
101It should have been in a halter.
102'Tis there; what's she?

FLAMINEO

'Tis there; what's she? Vittoria, my lord.

BRACHIANO

103Ha, ha, ha. Her hair is sprinkled with arras powder, that makes her look as if she sinn'd in the pastry. What's he?

FLAMINEO

104A divine my lord.

BRACHIANO

105He will be drunk. Avoid him: th'argument is fearful when
106churchmen stagger in't.
107Look you; six gray rats have lost their tails,
108Crawl up the pillow; send for a rat-catcher.
109I'll do a miracle: I'll free the court
110From all foul vermin. Where's Flamineo?

FLAMINEO

111I do not like that he names me so often,
112Especially on's death-bed: 'tis a sign
113I shall not live long: see he's near his end.

BRACHIANO seems here near is end

LODOVICO and GASPARO in the habit of Capuchins present him in his bed with a crucifix and hallowed candle.

LODOVICO

114Pray give us leave: Attende Domine Brachiane.

FLAMINEO

115See, see, how finaly he doth fix his eye
116Upon the crucifix.

VITTORIA

Upon the crucifix. O hold it constant.
117It settles his wild spirits; and so his eyes
118Melt into tears.

LODOVICO

119(By the crucifix) Domine Brachiane, solebas in bello tutus esse tuo clypeo, nùnc hanc clypeum hosti tui opponas ingernali.

GASPARO

120(By the hallowed taper) Olim hastâ valausti in bello; nûnc hanc sacram hastam vibrabis contra hostem animarum.

LODOVICO

121Attende Domine Brachiane si nunc quòque probas ea quæ acta sunt inter nos, flecte caput in dextrum.

GASPARO

122Esto securus. Domine Brachiane: cogita quantum habeas meritorum – denique memineris mean animam pro tua oppignoratam si quid esse periculi.

LODOVICO

123Si nùnc quoque probas ea quæ acta sunt inter nos, flecte caput in lævum.

124He is departing: pray stand all apart,
125And let us only whisper in his ears
126Some private meditations, which our order
127Permits you not to hear.

Here the rest being departed LODOVICO and GASPARO discover themselves

GASPARO

Permits you not to hear. Brachiano.

LODOVICO

128Devil Brachiano. Thou art damn'd.

GASPARO

Devil Brachiano. Thou art damn'd. Perpetually.

LODOVICO

129A slave condemn'd, and given up to the gallows
130Is thy great lord and master.

GASPARO

Is thy great lord and master. True: for thou
131Art given up to the devil.

LODOVICO

Art given up to the devil. O you slave!
132You that were held the famous politician;
133Whose art was poison.

GASPARO

Whose art was poison. And whose conscience murder.

LODOVICO

134That would have broke your wife's neck down the stairs ere she was poison'd.

GASPARO

135That had your villainous sallets –

LODOVICO

136And fine embroidered bottles, and perfumes
137Equally mortal with a winter plague –

GASPARO

138Now there's mercury –

LODOVICO

Now there's mercury – And copperas –

GASPARO

Now there's mercury – And copperas – And quicksilver –

LODOVICO

139With other devilish pothecary stuff
140A-melting in your politic brains: dost hear?

GASPARO

141This is Count Lodovico.

LODOVICO

This is Count Lodovico. This Gasparo.
142And thou shalt die like a poor rogue.

GASPARO

And thou shalt die like a poor rogue. And stink
143Like a dead fly-blown dog.

LODOVICO

144And be forgotten before thy funeral sermon.

BRACHIANO

145Vittoria! Vittoria!

LODOVICO

Vittoria! Vittoria! O the cursed devil,
146Come to himself again! We are undone.

Enter VITTORIA and the ATTEND[ANTS]

GASPARO

147[aside to LODOVICO] Strangle him in private.
148[to VITTORIA] What? Will you call him again
149To live in treble torments? For charity,
150For Christian charity, avoid the chamber.

Exeunt [VITTORIA and ATTENDANTS]

LODOVICO

151You would prate, sir. This is a true-love knot
152BRACHIANO is strangled Sent from the Duke of Florence.

GASPARO

BRACHIANO is strangled Sent from the Duke of Florence. What, is it done?

LODOVICO

153The snuff is out. No woman-keeper i'th' world,
154Though she had practis'd seven year at the pest-house,
155Could have done't quaintlier.

[Enter VITTORIA, FRANCISCO, FLAMINEO and ATTENDANTS]

Could have done't quaintlier. My lords he's dead.

OMNES

156Rest to his soul.

VITTORIA

Rest to his soul. O me! This place is hell.

Exit VITTORIA

[with ATTENDANTS and GASPARO]

FRANCISCO

157How heavily she takes it.

FLAMINEO

How heavily she takes it. O yes, yes;
158Had women navigable rivers in their eyes
159They would dispend them all; surely I wonder
160Why we should wish more rivers to the city
161When they sell water so good cheap. I'll tell thee,
162These are but moonish shades of griefs or fears,
163There's nothing sooner dry than women's tears.
164Why here's an end of all my harvest, he has given me nothing.
165Court promises! Let wise men count them curs'd
166For while you live he that scores best pays worst.

FRANCISCO

167Sure, this was Florence' doing.

FLAMINEO

Sure, this was Florence' doing. Very likely.
168Those are found weighty strokes which come from th'hand,
169But those are killing strokes which come from th'head.
170O the rare tricks of a Machivillian!
171He doth not come like a gross plodding slave
172And buffet you to death. No, my quaint knave,
173He tickles you to death; makes you die laughing;
174As if you had swallow'd down a pound of saffron.
175You see the feat, 'tis practis'd in a trice:
176To teach court-honesty, it jumps on ice.

FRANCISCO

177Now have the people liberty to talk
178And descant on his vices.

FLAMINEO

And descant on his vices. Misery of princes,
179That must of force be censur'd by their slaves!
180Not only blam'd for doing things are ill,
181But for not doing all that all men will.
182One were better be a thresher.
183Ud's death, I would fain speak with this Duke yet.

FRANCISCO

184Now he's dead?

FLAMINEO

185I cannot conjure; but if prayers or oaths
186Will get to th'speech of him: though forty devils
187Wait on him in his livery of flames,
188I'll speak to him, and shake him by the hand,
189Exit FLAMINEO Though I be blasted.

FRANCISCO

Exit FLAMINEO Though I be blasted. Excellent Lodovico!
190What? Did you terrify him at the last gasp?

LODOVICO

191Yes; and so idly, that the Duke had like
192T'have terrified us.

FRANCISCO

T'have terrified us. How?

Enter [ZANCHE] the Moor

LODOVICO

193You shall hear that hereafter.
194See! yon's the infernal that would make us sport.
195Now to the revelation of that secret
196She promis'd when she felt in love with you.

FRANCISCO

197You're passionately met in this sad world.

ZANCHE

198I would have you look up, sir; these court tears
199Claim not your tribute to them. Let those weep
200That guilty partake in the sad cause.
201I knew last night by a sad dream I had
202Some mischief would ensue; yet yo say truth
203My dream most concern'd you.

LODOVICO

My dream most concern'd you. Shall's fall a-dreaming?

FRANCISCO

204Yes, and for fashion sake I'll dream with her.

ZANCHE

205Methough sir, you came stealing to my bed.

FRANCISCO

206Wilt thou believe me sweeting? By this light
207I was a-dreamt on thee too: for methought
208I saw thee naked.

ZANCHE

I saw thee naked. Fie sir! as I told you,
209Methought you lay down by me.

FRANCISCO

Methought you lay down by me. So dreamt I:
210And lest thou shouldst take cold, I cover'd thee
211With this Irish mantle.

ZANCHE

With this Irish mantle. Verily I did dream,
212You were somewhat bold with me; but to come to't.

LODOVICO

213How? How? I hope you will not go to't here.

FRANCISCO

214Nay: you mist hear my dream out.

ZANCHE

Nay: you mist hear my dream out. Well, sir, forth.

FRANCISCO

215When I threw the mantle o'er thee, thou didst laugh
216Exceedingly methought.

ZANCHE

Exceedingly methought. Laugh?

FRANCISCO

Exceedingly methought. Laugh? And cried'st out,
217The hair did tickle thee.

ZANCHE

The hair did tickle thee. There was a dream indeed.

LODOVICO

218Mark her I prithee, she simpers like the suds
219A collier hath been wash'd in.

ZANCHE

220Come, sir; good fortune tends you; I did tell you
221I would reveal a secret: Isabella
222The Duke of Florence' sister was empoison'd,
223By a fum'd picture: and Camillo's neck
224Was broke by damn'd Flamineo; the mischance
225Laid on a vaulting-horse.

FRANCISCO

Laid on a vaulting-horse. Most strange!

ZANCHE

Laid on a vaulting-horse. Most strange! Most true.

LODOVICO

226The bed of snakes is broke.

ZANCHE

227I sadly do confess I had a hand
228In the black deed.

FRANCISCO

In the black deed. Thou kept'st their counser, –

ZANCHE

In the black deed. Thou kept'st their counser, – Right.
229For which urg'd with contrition, I intend
230This night to rob Vittoria.

LODOVICO

This night to rob Vittoria. Excellent penitence!
231Usurers dream on't while they sleep out sermons.

ZANCHE

232To further out escape, I have entreated
233Leave to retire me, till the funeral
234Unto a frien i'th' country. That excuse
235Will futher our escape. In coin and jewels
236I shall, at least, make good unto your use
237A hundred thousand crowns.

FRANCISCO

A hundred thousand crowns. O noble wench!

LODOVICO

238Those crowns we'll share.

ZANCHE

Those crowns we'll share. It is a dowry,
239Methinks, should make that sunburnt proverb false,
240And wash the Ethiop white.

FRANCISCO

And wash the Ethiop white. It shall, away!

ZANCHE

241Be ready for our flight.

FRANCISCO

Be ready for our flight. An hour 'fore day.

Exit [ZANCHE] the Moor

242O strange discovery! Why till now we knew not
243The circumstance of either of their deaths

Enter [ZANCHE the] Moor

ZANCHE

244You'll wait about midnight in the chapel?

FRANCISCO

You'll wait about midnight in the chapel? There.

LODOVICO

245Why now our action's justified, –

FRANCISCO

Why now our action's justified, – Tush for justice.
246What harms it justice? We now, like the partridge
247Purge the disease with laurel: for the fame
248Shall crown the enterprise and quit the shame.

Exeunt

[Act V, Scene iv]

Enter FLAM[INEO] and GASP[ARO] at one door, another way GIOVANNI attended

GASPARO

1The young Duke. Did you e'er see a sweeter prince?

FLAMINEO

2I have known a poor woman's bastard better favour'd. This is behind him. Now, to his face: all comparisons were hateful. Wise was the courtly peacock, that being a great minion, and being compar'd for beauty, by some dottrels that bird than herself, not in respect of her feathers, but in respect of her long tallants. His will grow out in time. My gracious lord.

GIOVANNI

3I pray leave me sir.

FLAMINEO

4Your Grace must be merry; 'tis I have cause to mourn; for wot you what said the little boy that rode behind his father on horseback?

GIOVANNI

5Why, what said he?

FLAMINEO

6'When you are dead father,' said he, 'I hope then I shall ride in the saddle.' O 'tis a brave thing for a man to sit by himself: he may stretch himself in the stirrups, look about, and see the whole compass of the hemisphere; you're now, my lord, i'th'saddle.

GIOVANNI

7Study your prayers, sir, and be penitent.
8‘Twere fit you’d think on what hath former been;
9I have heard grief named the eldest child of sin.

(Vanse Giovanni, Gasparo y acompañantes)

FLAMINEO

10Study my prayers? He threatens me divinely; I am falling to pieces already; I care not, though, like Anacharsis I were pounded to death in a mortar. And yet that death were fitter for usurers' gold and themselves to be beaten together, to make a most cordial cullis for the devil.

11He hath his uncle's villainous look already,
12Enter COURTIER In decimo-sexto. Now sir, what are you?

COURTIER

13It is the pleasure sir, of the young Duke
14That you forbear the presence, and all rooms
15That owe him reverence.

FLAMINEO

That owe him reverence. So, the wolf and the raven
16Are very pretty fools when they are young.
17Is it your office, sir, to keep me out?

COURTIER

18So the Duke wills.

FLAMINEO

19Verily, master courtier, extremity is not to be used in all offices. Say that a gentlewoman were taken out of her bed about midnight, and committed to Castle Angelo, to the tower yonder, with nothing about her, but her smock: would it not show a cruel part in the gentleman porter to lay claim to her upper garment, pull it o'er her head and ears; and put her in naked?

COURTIER

20Very good: you are merry.

[Exit]

FLAMINEO

21Doth he make a court ejectment of me? A flaming firebrand casts more smoke

22Enter [FRANCISCO, Duke of] Florence How now? Thou art sad.

FRANCISCO

23I met even now with the most piteous sight.

FLAMINEO

24Thou met'st another here, a pitiful
25Degraded courtier.

FRANCISCO

Degraded courtier. Your reverend mother
26Is grown a very old woman in two hours.
27I found them winding of Marcello's corse;
28And there is such a solemn melody
29'Tween doleful songs, tears, and sad elegies:
30Such as old grandames, watching by the dead,
31Were wont t'outwear the nights with; that belive me
32I had no eyes to guide me forth the room,
33They were so o'ercharg'd with water.

FLAMINEO

They were so o'ercharg'd with water. I will see them.

FRANCISCO

34'Twere much uncharity in you: for your sight
35Will add unto their tears.

FLAMINEO

Will add unto their tears. I will see them.

FRANCISCO

36They are behind the traverse. I'll discover
37[Draws the traverse] Their superstitious howling.

CORNELIA, [ZANCHE] the Moor and 3. other Ladies discovered, winding MARCELLO'S corse. A song.

CORNELIA

38This rosemary is wither'd, pray det fresh;
39I would have these herbs grow up in his grave
40When I am dead and rotten. Reach the bays,
41I'll tie a garland here about his head:
42'Twill keep my boy from lightning. This sheet
43I have kept this twenty year, and every day
44Hallow'd it with my prayers; I did not think
45He should have wore it.

ZANCHE

He should have wore it. Look you; who are yonder?

CORNELIA

46O reach me the flowers.

ZANCHE

47Her ladyship's foolish.

WOMAN

Her ladyship's foolish. Alas her grief
48Hath turn'd her child again.

CORNELIA

Hath turn'd her child again. to FLAMINEO You're very welcome.
49There's rosemary for you, and rue for you,
50Hearth's-ease for you. I pray make much of it.
51J have left more for myself.

FRANCISCO

J have left more for myself. Lady, who's this?

CORNELIA

52You are, I take it, the grave-maker.

FLAMINEO

You are, I take it, the grave-maker. So.

ZANCHE

53'Tis Flamineo.

[CORNELIA takes his hand]

CORNELIA

54Will you make me such a fool? Here's a white hand:
55Can blood so soon be wash'd out? Let me see:
56When screech-owls croak upon the chimney tops,
57And the strange cricket i'th' oven sings and hops,
58When yellow spots do on your hand appear,
59Be certain then you of a corse shall hear.
60Out upon't, how 'tis speckled! H'as handled a toad sure.
61Cowslip-water is good for the memory:
62Pray buy me 3. ounces of't.

FLAMINEO

63I would I were from hence.

CORNELIA

I would I were from hence. Do you hear, sir?
64I'll give you a saying which my grandmother
65Was wont, when she heard the bell toll, to sing o'er
66Unto her lute –

FLAMINEO

Unto her lute – Do and you will, do.

CORNELIA doth this in several forms of distraction

CORNELIA

67Call for the robin red breast and the wren,
68Since o'er shady groves they hover,
69And with leaves and flow'rs do cover
70The friendless bodies of unburied men.
71Call unto his funeral dole
72The ant, the field-mouse, and the mole
73To rear him hillocks, that shall keep him warm
74And (when gay tombs are robb'd) sustain no harm,
75But keep the wolf far thence: that's foe to men,
76For with his nails he'll dig them up again.
77They would not bury him 'cause he died in a quarrel
78But I have an answer for them.
79Let holy church receive him duly
80Since he paid the church tithes truly.
81His wealth is summ'd, and this is all his store:
82This poor men get; and great men get no more.
83Now the wares are gone, we may shut up shop.
84Bless you all good people.

Exeunt CORNELIA [, ZANCHE] and Ladies

FLAMINEO

85I have a strange thing in me, to the which
86I cannot give a name, without it be
87Exit FRANCISCO Compassion; I pray leave me.
88This night I'll know the utmost of my fate,
89I'll be resolv'd what my rich sister means
90T'assign me for my service. I have liv'd
91Riotously ill, like some that live in court.
92And sometimes, when my face was full of smiles
93Have felt the maze of conscience in my breast.
94Oft gay and honour'd robes those tortures try,
95We think cag'd birds sing, when indeed they cry.

Enter BRACHIA[NO'S] Ghost. In his leather cassock and breeches, boots, a cowl [and in his hand] a pot of lily-flowers with a skull in't.

96Ha! I can stand thee. Nearer, nearer yet.
97What a mockery hath death made of thee? Thou look'st sad.
98In what place art thou? In yon starry gallery,
99Or in the cursed dungeon? No? not speak?
100Pray, sir, resolve me, what religion's best
101For a man to die in? or is it in your knowledge
102To answer me how long I have to live?
103That's the most necessary question.
104Not answer? Are you still like some great men
105That only walk like shadows up and down,
106And to no purpose: say: ——
107The ghost throws earth upon him and shows him the skull
108What's that? O fatal! He throws earth upon me.
109A dead man's skull beneath the roots of flowers.
110I pray speak sir; our Italian churchmen
111Make us believe, dead men hold conference
112With their familiars, and many times
113Exit Ghost Will come to bed to them, and eat with them.
114He's gone; and see, the skull and earth are vanish'd.
115This is beyond melancholy. I do dare my fate
116To do its worst. Now to my sister's lodging,
117And sum up all these horrors; the disgrace
118The Prince threw on me; next the piteous sight
119And last this terrible vision. All these
120Shall with Vittoria's bounty turn togood,
121Or I will drown this weapon in her blood.

Exit

[Act V, Scene v]

Enter FRANCISCO, LODOVICO, and HORTENSIO [overhearing them]

LODOVICO

1My lord upon my soul you shall no further:
2You have most ridiculously engag'd yourself
3Too far already. For my part, I have paid
4All my debts, so if I should chance to fall
5My creditors fall not with me; and I vow
6To quite all in this bold assembly
7To the meanest follower. My lord eave the city,
8Or I'll forswear the murder.

FRANCISCO

Or I'll forswear the murder. Farewell Lodovico.
9If thou dost perish in this glorious act,
10I'll rear unto thy memory that fame
11Shall in the ashes keep alive thy name.

[Exeunt FRANCISCO and LODOVICO]

HORTENSIO

12There's some black deed on foot. I'll presently
13Down to the citadel, and raise some force.
14These strong court factions that do brook no checks,
15In the career oft break the riders' necks.

[Exit]

[Act V, Scene vi]

Enter VITTORIA with a book in her hand, ZANCHE; FLAMINEO following them

FLAMINEO

1What, are you at your prayers? Give o'er.

VITTORIA

What, are you at your prayers? Give o'er. How ruffin?

FLAMINEO

2I come to you 'bout worldly business:
3Sit down, sit down. Nay, stay blouze, you may hear it,
4The doors are fast enough.

VITTORIA

The doors are fast enough. Ha, are you drunk?

FLAMINEO

5Yes, yes, with wormwood water; you shall taste
6Some of it presently.

VITTORIA

Some of it presently. What intends the fury?

FLAMINEO

7You are my lord's executrix, and I claim
8Reward, for my long service.

VITTORIA

Reward, for my long service. For your service?

FLAMINEO

9Come therefore, here is pen and ink, set down
10What you will give me.

She writes

VITTORIA

11There.

FLAMINEO

There. Ha! have you done already?
12'Tis a most short conveyance.

VITTORIA

'Tis a most short conveyance. I will read it.
13[reads] I give that portion to thee, and no other
14Which Cain groan'd under having slain his brother.

FLAMINEO

15A most courtly patent to beg by.

VITTORIA

A most courtly patent to beg by. You are a villain.

FLAMINEO

16Is't come to this? They say affrights cure agues;
17Thou hast a devil in thee; I will try
18If I can scare him from thee. Nay sit still:
19My lord hath left me yet two caso of jewels
20Shall make me scorn you bounty; you shall see them.

[Exit]

VITTORIA

21Sure he's distracted.

ZANCHE

Sure he's distracted. O he's desperate!
22For your own safety give him gentle language.

He enters with two case of pistols

FLAMINEO

23Look, these are better far at a dead lift,
24Than all your jewel house.

VITTORIA

Than all your jewel house. And yet methinks,
25These stones have no fair lustre, they are ill set.

FLAMINEO

26I'l turn the right side towards you: you shall see
27How they will sparkle.

VITTORIA

How they will sparkle. Turn this horror from me:
28What do you want? What would you have me do?
29Is not all mine, yours? Have I any children?

FLAMINEO

30Pray thee good woman do not trouble me
31With this vain worldly business; say your prayers;
32I made a vow to my deceased lord,
33Neither yourself, nor I should outlive him,
34The numb'ring of four hours.

VITTORIA

The numb'ring of four hours. Did he enjoin it?

FLAMINEO

35He did, and 'twas a deadly jealousy,
36Lest any should enjoy thee after him,
37That urg'd him vow me to it. For my death,
38I did propound it voluntarily, knowing
39If he could not be safe in his own court
40Being a great Duke, what hope then for us?

VITTORIA

41This is your melancholy and despair.

FLAMINEO

This is your melancholy and despair. Away;
42Fool that thou art to think that politicians
43Do use to kill the effects of injuries
44And let the cause live: shall we groan in irons,
45Or be a shameful and a weight burthen
46To a public scaffold? This is my resolve:
47I would not live at any man's entreaty
48Nor die at any's bidding.

VITTORIA

Nor die at any's bidding. Will you hear me?

FLAMINEO

49My life hath done service to other men,
50My death shall serve mine own turn; make you ready.

VITTORIA

51Do you mean to die indeed?

FLAMINEO

Do you mean to die indeed? With as much pleasure
52As e’er my father gat me..

VITTORIA

As e’er my father gat me.. [aside to ZANCHE] Are the doors lock’d?

ZANCHE

53Yes madam.

VITTORIA

54Are you grown an atheist? Will you turn your body,
55Which is the goodly palace of the soul
56To the soul’s slaughter house? O the cursed devil
57Which doth present us with all other sins
58Thrice candied o’er; despair with gall and stibium, [aside to ZANCHE] Cry out for help.
59Yet we carouse it off;
60Makes us forsake that which was made for man,
61The world, to sink to that was made for devils,
62Eternal darkness.

ZANCHE

Eternal darkness. Help, help!

FLAMINEO

Eternal darkness. Help, help! I’ll stop your throat
63With winter plums, —

VITTORIA

With winter plums, — I prithee yet remember,
64Millions are now in graves, which at last day
65Like mandrakes shall rise shrieking.

FLAMINEO

Like mandrakes shall rise shrieking. Leave your prating,
66For these are but grammatical laments,
67Feminine arguments, and they move me
68As some in pulpits move their auditory
69More with their exclamation than sense
70Of reason, or sound doctrine.

ZANCHE

Of reason, or sound doctrine. [aside] Gentle madamaparte
71Seem to consent, only persuade him teach
72The way to death; let him die first.

VITTORIA

73[aside] ‘Tis good, I apprehend it. —aparte
74To kill oneself is meat that we must take
75Like pills, not chew’t, but quickly swallow it;
76The smart o’th’ wound, or weakness of the hand
77May else bring treble torments.

FLAMINEO

May else bring treble torments. I have held it
78A wretched and most miserable life,
79Which is not able to die.

VITTORIA

Which is not able to die. O but frailty!
80Yet I am now resolv’d; farewell affliction.
81Behold Brachiano, I that while you liv’d
82Did make a flaming altar of my heart
83To sacrifice unto you; now am ready
84To sacrifice heart and all. Farewell Zanche.

ZANCHE

85How madam! Do you think that I’ll outlive you?
86Expecially when my best self Flamineo
87Goes the same voyage.

FLAMINEO

Goes the same voyage. O most loved Moor!

ZANCHE

88Only, by all my love let me entreat you;
89Since it is most necessary none of us
90Do violence in ourselves; let you or I
